Through the politeness of a gentleman in town we have been kindly favored with a copy of the following letter, which gives an account of the facts connected with the sad ravages of Cholera in St. Kitts. There is a remedy given in the latter part of the letter, hut we cannot vouch lor its good effects. þÿ St. Kitts, November 29, 1854. I write yon a few linos to relieve your anxie ties concerning us, for you will of course have heard that Cholera is amongst us. No Island could have spent more rigid quarantine more money in sanitary than this regulations has done, or enforced and yet it has broken out amongst us with as great violence, a» if wo had taken no pains at all. There can be no doubt that its cause is atmospheric, and every person choleraically disposed, or in a very bilious condition is liable to its attack. 1 do not find that it is contagious during illness ; of course prudence is required, and disinfecting fluids are best; but there need not be that foolish running away from person a attacked. After death of course the sooner the body is buried the better. If it unfortunately visits you, as I fear it will, your system as regards the laborers for your þÿestates doctor could previously examine tlio whole gang and take the names of those found to require active ment, so quail fv |he negro tor n more medicines and by their preventive favorable attack, treatif attacked at all. Tn our case the laborers do not reside on the estate, and for the most part live in the

3t, 0 3S 0 3 ATI 3. suburbs of towns, and as to doctors, they would die before they spent a farthing in that commodity and consequently they are almost to a man at this time surcharged with bile. They get the attack in the night and are dead before morning. The total deaths are about 1500 as yet. In town 50 to 60 a day ; it has reached 120. Calomel is the sheet-anchor, and a mixture of 1 oz. cloves, 1 oz. cinnamon, 1 oz. ginger, 1 oz. nutmeg, A oz. pounded pepper dissolved in a quart of Brandy is a good stomachic; a dessert spoonful to a half tumbler of hot sugar and water in the dose. It keeps heat in the body and promotes perspiration. þÿ

The following has been kindly communicated to us : The Danish Corvette IVayaden has very recently visited the Island of Aves (Birds Island) and the result of her visit is as follows : The Island is taken possession of by two American Captains, bang and Gibbs, who have resided there since last June with 50 laborers, colored and white, built tents and a landing place ; and have provided themselves with hoats for loading and unloading vessels which come to the Island. As they are the first who discovered Guano on the Island and as they have gone to no inconsiderable expense, they consider themselves justified Guano venting others from taking away in prefrom the Island ; hut they are willing to dispose of it at five dollars pr. ot ton, brought free of charge to the side the vessel. During the Corvette's stay there, three three-masted vessels and a Brig were at anchor to take in Guano. The Island is very small, anil the demand for Guano being great, the enterprise in all probability will he over in the course of one or two years. The Guano found on the Island is of two qualities, samples of which are brought to this Island, and can he seen at the Custom House here in boxes marked No. 1 and 2. No.l is considered by bang and Gibbs to he the best.

The Royal Mail Steam-ship Atrata, Captain Wooi.ley, arrived here at 9 o'clock on Thursday 1 night with the European Mails Senor Corraps

Setti, with a Company of Opera Singers þÿ whose expected arrival we announced on the 18th ult þÿ came passeDgers by this fine steamer. Included in the Atrato's items of news we believe we are warranted in stating that the Company's ships Thames, Tamar, and Magdalena had been taken up by the British Government to convey French troops to the East, and would with all possible speed be sent forthwith to Toulon. Such was the despatch manifested, that, whilst the homeward cargo of the Thames was being discharged over the one side, Stores for the Troops were being taken in at the other. And such of the officers and crew as would not sign Articles for two years were being paid off at one end of a table, while those who were willing to ship for that period were receiving advances at the other. It is certain that there will be no West India Mail for the 17th December, and it is more than questionable if there will be one for the þÿ2nd this day. Here, then, may say, we that for the first, we begin to realize tlie consequences of the War that is now over-shadowing Europe, and brings to light practically the nature of its magnitude. The appointment bears date the 11th of the same month ; and the new Governor was
to proceed to the West Indies in the early part of next year, to replace Governor Feddersen, who had expressed a wish to return to Europe. þÿ Ibid December 2.

To I lie F<li(or of' flie " Tiilemle." Dear Sir. þÿ Landing at the King's Wharf on the evening of the 30th ult. from on hoard the Steamer " Atrato," whither I had proceeded to meet some friends expected from England by that vessel, I witnessed an accident, which might have had grave consequences; as it was, it came off merely with the thorough soaking in the water of Mr. 1. G. Knight, Junior, passenger from the " Atrato." This gentleman had scarcely put his foot on the wharf, after having happily arrived from Europe, when suddenly turning round to salute an acquaintance, he fell backwards and disappeared under the wharf. Luckily the moon was bright and the persons present were enabled to extricate him from a perilous position, without his having suffered seriously by the fall. Now, Sir, since the month of October last, ihe two Scuttles to the south end of the King's wharf have been destroyed by the violence of the weather, (part of one still lying unremoved, where it was placed by the waves), and as far as I am aware nothing has as yet been done in order to repair them and fix Ihe only public landing place in (he Island, in such a stale as fo render it safe for the use of the many who are daily coming and going. Pray Sir, can you inform me what measures have been, or arc likely to he, taken, so as to remedy such an evil, not only dangerous to limbs hut to ? life, par- ticularly so on a dark evening I cannot presume it be from want of knowledge of the real state of things,

that the necessary repairs have not been effected long ere this, because it must be palpably to any one who visits the spof. It is certainly to be regretted, that in a place like this, our only public quay should he neglected in such a manner. I am, Mr. Editor, Your most obedient servant, H. St. Thomas, 2nd December, 1854.

From the Antigua Observer, November 9. The long talked of Exhibition of Industry is at length an accomplished fact, a tangible, existing reality, and whatever doubts may have been previously entertained of the industrial capabilities and public spun of the islands, people of Antigua, and of some of now such doubts may fairly the adjacent be resolved into the conviction, that all are not so deeply sunk in the mire of utter wotihlessness as has been sometimes represented. The dis play of articles at this gaihering has been on the whole creditable, and we are free to con less, has surpassed our expectations So coin mon is it for projects of various kinds to be started in Antigua, to be largely talked of for a time, and then to be totally forgotten, that very many persons anticipated the failure ol tfie present undertaking ; and the prevalence of such an impression occasioned no doubt considerable backwardness in support of the scheme, the dubious class forgetting altogether, that their own individual exertions were wanting to further and ensure the desir ed result. But notwithstanding the undoubted operation of this feeling general!) ; sufficient lias been done to demonstrate that the combined energies of even a few individuals may produce results of no insignificant kind, and after all, the Exhibition may be justly deemed a successful realization of the objects of its pro jcclors. To the sceptical it has afforded evidence that much, even in Antigua, may be accomplished with a little determination ; to the enterprising and industrious, we hope it

will be substantially evinced, ere the Exhibition closes, that their labors can lie appreciated ; while to the apathetic and despaning, a wholesome stimulus, we trust, lias been ap plied to rouse them to exertion. Opening ol' tlic Royal Banish Railway. ( From the Illustrated London News.) In our Journal of the 7th of last month we gave some details and illustrations of the inauguration of the Norwegian Grand Trunk, then recently completed by Mr. S. M. Feto, M.P., and bis associate contractors and capitalists, for King Oscar and the Government of that country. We have now the no less agreeable duty of recording a still further de-

Q'&D'l'JL A 'H 3 velopment of railway progress among the populations of the Scandinavian kingdoms, through the same British instrumentality, and a still more emphatic Royal recognition þÿof the services so conferred on our northern neighbours by our enterprising countryman, the member for Norwich, and his colleagues. The þÿ Royal þÿDanish was opened by Frcderik VII., Kingof Denmark, hisleading Ministers, and the dignitaries of his Court, on Oct. 25th, under circumstances that left nothing to he desired, whether as regards the eclat that surrounded the festivities in the eyes of the Danish Sovereign and li is subjects, or the proofs afforded of the soundness of the original expectations of the projectors as to the line being availed of by the trading and travelling classes, to the consequent prospective remuneration of the proprietary. Mr. þÿPeto s party consisted of Mr. G. P. Bidder, the Engineer of the line, and his collaboratcur, Mr. G. Stephenson ; Mr. J. Anderson, Deputy Chairman ; and Mr. F. Gooch, the zealous Secretary of the þÿ Royal þÿDanish Company; Mr. J. V. Gooch, Superintendent of the EastþÿDanish locomotives); together with ern Counties (builder of the þÿ Royal 21st Messrs. Laurence and Rich, and others, the private guests of Mr. Peto. These gentlemen left Lowestoft on Saturday morning, the 19th lilt., on board the North of Europe Steam Navigation Comþÿpany s vessel Cygnus, Capt. Raymond, R. N., but specially þÿ presided þÿover, so to speak on this occasion, by the Com-

þÿpany M s anager, Capt. VV. S. Andrews. As the þÿ Majesty of þÿDenmark was to be entertained on board, the Cygnus was provisioned with delicacies worthy of the regalement of a King, and with all the necessary appliances for serving them with befitting elegance and splendour. Mr. Ilowett, proprietor of the Royal Hotel, Lowestoft, whence the repast was furnished, personally superintended the arrangements of the tables. The vessel was further provided with a profusion of gorgeous streamers, flags, and banners. These, when subsequently unfurled in Tonning harbour, had an effect altogether unique amid the adornments of a like kind which all the craft in the port exhibited ; and she further carried with her an assortment of fireworks þÿ not only sufficient for her own feuxdejoie, but which permitted the inhabitants of Flensborg to be favoured with a pyrotechnic display which much delighted the natives ; between whom and the English the best possible feeling exists. This is owing, not only to the English capital poured into their country both by the formation of the line, and by the North of Europe Steam Company opening up numerous British markets for native produce, but to the conciliatory spirit and excellent tact of all the English railway officials and employes resident in Denmark. Though the weather was anything hut calm, the Cygnus made the run in twenty-six hours from Lowestoft to Tonning. In this commodious and finely situated coast terminus of the Railway, the be-

nefits of its position are becoming evident in its being the marine bead-quarters of the fast-growing traffic between the two countries. It is by way of Tonning that the capital of Denmark and consequently nearly all the Baltic ports, may be reached with a great saving of time, distance, and inconvenience, as compared with any other existing or possible route ; and not only in summer but in winter, when Copenhagen is inaccessible by water, via Hull ; while by the junction which the Royal Danish effects with the Kiel and Altona lines all those great arteries of German and | Prussian Railway Continental commu-

nication radiating from Hamburg, may be said to be placed at the command of the Danes. Moreover, it is at Tonning that are concentrated for exportation at Lowestoft, and thence direct for London, after having been fattened on their pastures, those immense herds of cattle which stud the fertile plains of Jutland. These animals likewise contribute to the exports of Tonning a most important item þÿ namely, butter; the increase of which between 1851 and 1853, lias been from 307 to 164,887 tubs. In the same period the exportation of sheep lias risen from 5,623 to 16,134; and at the expiration of the current year this ratio will have been far surpassed : while the trade in wheat and cereal produce generally is also augmenting in a like degree. Hence, with so prosperous a present it is obvious bow flourishing a future is in store for this thriving port. The line is carried to its very jetty, ns is also the case at Lowestoft þÿ a most important arrangement for preserving the cattle from deterioration though having to be driven any distance either before or after being on ship-board. Having duly inspected the town, the English party started at noon on the from Tonning þÿ thirty miles from Schleswig, and eleven from the mouth of the Eider þÿ for Flonsburg, forty-two miles inland, passing Ihrough the intermediate town of Husnm (population 5000). Flenshurg,containingnhout 18000 inhabitants, is n remarkably well-built, beautifully situated, and highly interesting town. It combines many of the most

quaint features of a mediicvel age, in the aspect of its buildings and the usages of its people, with evidences of an observant attention to modern improvements. By the overland route of the þÿ Royal þÿDanish a dangerous (and in winter impracticable) navigation þÿol five hundred miles by the Skew and Kattegat is saved, and with it the Sound dues amounting, on fine goods, to the whole transit cost by railway. The port charges at Flensburg are exceedingly small, and the facilities for all shipping purposes admirable þÿ the harbour being completely landlocked twenty miles from the coast, and their being ample depth of water, and no rise or fall of tide, requiring expensive contrivances for loading and unloading. The accommodations at þÿBach s Hotel, at which the English party stopped, show that Flensburg is quite on a par with towns of a like size in countries boasting of a more luxurious civilisation than Denmark, and it is in course of being lighted with gas. The Flcnshurgers were most enthusiastic in the loyalty of the reception of their King, in whose bononr, and that of his Consort, Louise Countess Danner, who accompanied him, immense preparations were made. Rejoicings of every kind were kept up incessantly tor the whole period he remained in the town and neighbourhood, nearly four days and nights. cy, Charles Comte, de Mnltke, Minister for the Duchy of Schleswig ; M. From theObserrerT October 29, 1854. LATEST FROM THE CRIMEA. ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH. VIENNA, FRIDAY, Oct. 27 Lord Burghersh arrived here yesterday. Advices have been received from Varna of the 21st October. The land batteries opened fire on Sebastopol on the 17th. The allied fleets did the same at the entrance ol the harbour, with success, but with the seveie loss of 90 killed and 300 wounded. The Agamemnon suffered most The Quarantine Fort was silenced. The fall of the city was expected to take place about the 25th. 30,000 French, under the orders of General Bosquet, have been or dered to cut off the communication between the north and south sides of Sebastopol. Report says that General Luders has brought 13,500 men to Sebastopol. Oihers, 12 000 Russians hold the heights of Belbek. On the 15th the reinforcements under l.iprandi were still at þÿl etekop The Inflexible and Sidon (English), with tfie Caton and Cacique (French), have been engaged at the mouth of the Dnieper in can nonading Russian forts, San Ninolao, and another in the town. The Russians fired hot shot at a distance of 5.600 yards, but the firing was not good, falling generally short of the mark, but at times the shot fell near and passed between the mast heads of the vessels engaged. Luckily the loss on our side was nothing. One of their shot went through the funnel of the Sidon. The principal object of the vessels taking up the position was to cut off the body of the relief marching towards Sebastopol. In this they were quite success ful. for they were turned at the Lake of Do-

vinoski, and again at the lake of Atjalik, and the squadron, following them along the coast, has not only harassed them very considerably, but has, as a matter of course, delayed from dav to day the union of the reinforcement to the besieged army in þÿSebastopol. Intelligence, which may be considered dc oisive, has at last reached this country of the sad fate of Sir John Franklin and his brave companions. Dr. Rae, whose previous exploits as an Arctic traveller have already so highly d is tinguished him, landed at Deal yesterday (Sunday), and immediately proceeded to the Admiralty, and laid before Sir James Graham the melancholy evidence on which his teport is founded. l)r. Rae was not employed in searching for Sir John Franklin, hut in completing his survey of the coast of Boothia. He justly thought, however, that the information lie had obtained greatly outweighed the importance of his survey, and he has hurried home to satisfy the public anxiety as to the fate of the long lost expedition, and to prevent the risk of any more lives in a fruitless search. It would seem from Ins description of the place in which the bodies were found that both Sir Janies Ross and Captain Bellot must have been within a few miles of the spot to which our unfortunate countrymen had snug gled on in their desperate march. A few of the unfoi lunate men must, tie thinks, have survived until the arrival of the wild fowl about the end of May, 1850, as shots wcic heard and fresh bones and feathers of geese were noticed near the scene of the sad event

We regret to learn that Cholera lias made its appearance in the Island of St. Christopher, where, report says, it is committing great ravages. This, if true, is very unpleasant news, and it would be well if the inhabitants of the neighboring islands at once adopt sanitary measures. We, therefore, suggest that a committee be appointed here, as was the case last year, when Cholera visited St. Thomas, and that the different yards he properly visited, no rubbish, hog pens, &.C., be allowed to remain there. Vacant lots ought also to he cleaned.

TRIM HAD. þÿ Out of evil often proceedeth þÿRood. The maxim is þÿtrite but what truthful one is not ? þÿ and ever is it receiving fresh and striking authenticaiions, from the events of everv dav existence. From how many hardly-borne calamities which have, at the time of their occurrence, been regarded as the sorest and most unmitigated afflictions, mani fold special advantages have been derived, to be the most valued blessings of future ages Few of these cruel affliction-generated reme dies have been more prominent than the de vastating plague from whose terrible irflu ence we are but now escaping. So striking have been its reforming powers, that the question has been often rnised hv far-seeing and pondering men, whether the Cholera has not, in reality, in many places, been n hies sing rather than a curse þÿ an instrument in the hands of an allwise Providence to raise us to the performance of those neglected duties which our present existence imperatively demands The reason of this, too, is obvious The activity of thought and action evoked in the absolute necessity, of watchful caution and the use of our utmost energies to avoid ahsolute destruction, is never fruitless never remains satisfied with allaying the mere necessity that called it into existence, þÿ but always. from the impulse given, lakes a siep or two farther in the onward path of progress : whence arise useful projects of social amelioration þÿ projects fructified into actual working institutions. Whilst we deplore (he dreadful mortality

which has attended the visit of the Epidemic to this þÿtown a mortality, ns far as we can learn, greater in proportion to the extent of the population, than in almost anv oiher citv subjected to the visitation, þÿ we cannot hot coincide in the opinion of strangers, who, after experience of its effects and of the efforts made to resist its attacks in other places þÿ unhesitatingly affirm, that in a few plare in tho world has it been met and combatted with more determination, and tesolute adoption of all precautionary and remedial measures ; and (hough, no don hi, a very heavy expense has been incurred, which the colonv is ill able to bear, we think that every one will be but too glad that a greater loss of life þÿ which is in the West Indies perhaps mote than any whete the sinews of prosperity has been averted by a large pecuniary sacrifice. Our loss is even now of terrible magnitude, imagination shrinks from picturing what it might have been had the disease been allowed to run its fell course unchecked by the numei rous barriers that medical skill, public enterprise, and private benevolence, have so time miltingly raised against its progress. Again, therefore, we repeat, that Fort of Spain has high reason for thankfulness and self gratitude in the midst of its deep affliction. And during the existence of such a feeling, wo think we cannot do better than point out a mode of manifesting its influence, and proving its sincerity, which appears to us moat desirable, and by which at the same
time, we may add another example of the

3 frequency of ultimate good proceeding from evil, by conferring a lasting benefit, and fulfil a duty which common charily imposes on us. To those who look into the statistics of humble life þÿ here as elsewhere þÿ the great problem is, what is the best, or what is even a tolerably good way of dealing with the children of the poorer classes? Flan after plan is discussed and experimented on, but as yet the problem is unsolved. In this Island it was a subject of paramount interest, which seriously engaged the attention of our late Governor Lord Harris, who brought to the consideration a mind at once astute and philanthropic, and a most ardent desire for the improvement of the population. We will not assert that the plans introduced and so warmly and unremittingly supported by him, have turned out failures ; but we most confidently do assert, that they fail in very many particulars to meet the necessities of the demand as manifested in this Island, and that, in fact the system, though most undoubtedly a very excellent one, leaves very much yet to be desired. '1 he subject receives a new impulse for dehbeiation, and a greater necessity of meeting and overcoming the difficulty, from the sad effects of the recent calamitous visitation. Out of the 2,000 deaths that have occurred within the last two months in Fort of Spain alone, it is a serious matter for thought how many of these were parents, or in other ways protectors of children, who must be now left quite destitute, or perhaps worse, left to the

interested care of those who will only bring them up in the paths of uselessness and vice. To rescue them from such a fate, and to provide them with an asylum and refuge, where thev mav not only be saved from want, and the too alluring example of vice and prema lure dissoluteness, but be reared as useful and worthy members of the community, arid be converted from a plague spot among the people into a healthy and desirable item of the population, is surely an object worthy the attention and efforts of nil, þÿ and as surely, if some plan for the accomplishment of such a consummation be carried out under the influence of the feelings or circumstances brought about by Cholera, we may hereafter have reason to be grateful instead of repining at its visitation. Let, then, all unite in a determined and earnest endeavour to strike out some feasible project having this object in view, and, having done that do our best to carry it out successfully and promptly. We will not pretend to point out any particular plan of action, but we offer a few hints and suggestions on the subject which it appears to us very necessary to hear in mind. In the first place, supposing a place of asylum in Fort of Spain, or, far preferable as we think, in some healthy and convenient spot at some distance from it, to be provided. The age of admittance and duration of stay are to he determined Leaving the first point, on the next we think that the earlier it is found possible for them to leave the asy-

lum, the belter : not that the managcis should therefore lose their power of directing and influencing their conduct to good We think this power (we use the word power advisably ) should extend some years after their personally quitting the asylum ; but that their education or training after this should fie carried on as circumstances might require, uninterfered with by the conductors of the asylum, unless in cases of dereliction from duty on either side. We think that by some such means the great obstacle to unanimity of support loan institution of this kind would be oveicnme þÿ we allude, of course, to the difference in religious doctrines, which exists in the town. Let it be understood that those

A 7 I 8 who are children of Roman Catholic parents, or children received into that Church by baptism, he placed with families of that communion, and the children of Protestants located with members of the Church of England, after their term of residence at the asylum lias transpired complete. To render this possible, a previous avoidance of all sectional teaching must be rigidly carried out, and we firmly believe tins may be done without injuriously affecting their inoial and devotional training In the second place comes the course of training and teaching which will be most beneficial to them and the colony j this of necessity trenches on the vexatu questio of the age. We think the golden rule is sum med up in the few words. " Avoid þÿextremes þÿ do not attempt to give them an education entirely unfitted to their future prospects þÿ columns. 1 1 we succeed in giving the imbut do not, on the other hand leave them without intellectual culture at all. The following extract from the report of Mr. Hornet bears very oppositely on the matter, and afford some valuable suggestions : þÿ þÿ The good that has been effected by the education clauses of the Factory Act wherever there is a really in this country of u legislative compulsory education, j possessing good school, is the happy result of the first trial made combined with an industrial employment of the children, that brings in wages to their parents ; and it does not appear to me to have received the attention it deserves from the earnest friends of the education of the

working classes. It has now been shown abundantly, by the experience of nearly twenty years, that it is quite possible to give, in half a day of regular attendance at school for three or four years, a very considerable amount of solid instruction, while at the same time a child can earn no small amount of its mainlenance, certainly more than sufiicicnt to clothe it well and pay for its education. There are numerous instances of children who, while working daily in ! the lactorv, and attending school one half of the day, have made such progress that they were able to stand successfully the strict examination for pupil teachers There appears to be a growing conviction, that until there has been a succession of educated I parents among the humbler classes, capable of appreciating the good to their children by a long and regular attendance at school, we never shall have them sent, if their parents can turn them to money account, small though the wages they got with them may be. It must, in some form or other, be made obligatory and the successful working of the Factory Act in ibis respect is a very successful beginning. It is a great fallacy, in mv opinion, to designate such an obligation as an unjustifiable interference with parental rights ; for, if such a law existed, it would be felt by those only who neglected their parental duties þÿ Mr. Horner's Factory Report. And the condition recommended by a committee appointed in one of the other islands, bears not the same views:

þÿ I. No person to be admitted or retained at school about 12 years of age. þÿ 2. A contribution to be exacted from all scholars ; to inculcate the value of Education. þÿ 3. Four days attendance in eacli week to be required. þÿ 4. Scriptural Instruction to form a principal feature in education. þÿ 5. The subjects taught to be Reading, Writing Arithmetic, the elements of Geography, and the n-e of the ordinary agricultural and mechanical implements. þÿ 6. Prizes to be given for proficiencies ; rewards at the end of the term of tuition, to be expended for advancement in a trade, or in the purchase of tools ; or to secure further education, in the case of scholars who have exhibited during their course of training extraordinary qualifications." Certainly, the directors of the asylum must he endued with full legal discretionary powers of controul over those they support, not only during their stay in the asylum, hut extending to some I years into their after life. The universal complaint amongst those who have, from the most charitable motives, taken to their homes young destitute children, and with infinite pains and no little vexation of spirit, supported them through their useless infancy, is, that the moment they begin to reap the success of their educational efforts, and derive some benefit of the services of their protegees, they lose them altogether, as they are constantly decoyed away by their quasi friends. If this liability, as well as the previous early teaching and most difficult part
of the bringing up, can he removed by the authority of the asylum, we have no doubt many respectable housekeepers

will he hut too glad to carry on their training alter leaving ihe asylum as domestic servants, and willingly pay a premium tor their sevices. Hence might he raised a number of superior seiv.mts, than whom few classes of people are in greater requisition ; and twe believe that in this direction the attempts of the institution would be most likely to succeed, þÿ the extreme youth of the children would preclude the possihiliy of te. idling them the details ot field labour, þÿ and from the funds der i v i d from this source sufficient provision might he made to carry on the institution on an almost self-supporting basis. The subject is a most important one and embraces very many conflicting components hoi few of which can, of couise, he touched, hardy touched upon in our

pel us of motion in the matter, we shall he fully satisfied, and doubt not hut that the details will he satisfactorily arranged. So we end as we began, by earnestly calling the attention of the charitable to the matter, and entreating them in the name of suffering humanity, in the most preform þÿ little children þÿ to give the subject early and productive consideration. þÿ Fort of Spain Gazette.

Dickens tells the following slory of an American sea captain : þÿ In Ins last voyage home, the captain had on hoard a young lady of remarkable personal attractions þÿ a phrase I use as being one entirely new, and one you never meet with in the newspapers. This young lady was beloved intensely by live young gentlemen, passengers, and in turn she was in love with them all very ardently, hut without any particular preference for either. Not knowing how to make up her determination in this dilemma, she consulted my friend the captain. 'Fhe captain, being a man of original turn of mind, says lo the young lady, þÿ jump overboard, and marry the man who jumps after þÿyou. The young lady struck with the idea, and being fond of bathing, especially in warm weather, as it then Was, took the advice of the captain, who had a boat ready and manned in case of accident. Accordingly next morning, the five lovers being on deek, and looking devoutedly at the young lady, she plunged into the sea head foremost. Four of the lovers immediately jumped in after her. When the young lady and her four lovers got out again, she says to the captain, þÿ What am I to do now, they are so þÿwet? Says the captain þÿ Take I he dry one þÿ! And the young lady did, and married him.

and to forward its proposals to the superior authority, conformably the provisions in the Re- to script of 8th April 1768 paragraph þÿ2. With regard to the contents of the 18th and succeeding paragraphs of the draft relative to the assessment of taxes it must bo observed, that all the seven members of the Committee appointed to deliberate on the draft as well as the Colonial Council in toto agree upon, that all that the draft contains in regard of the assessments on the inhabitants, according to their fortune and circumstances, of the annual expenses of the Commune (in as far as these are not covered by the taxes imposed by the laws) ought at all events to be eliminated. Notwithstanding such a system of assessment is warranted by the Rescript ol 8th April 1 768 for St. Croix, it has never been enforced To revive this antiquated regulation by inserting it in a general municipal ordinance for all the islands at a period when all the Landtrcasurics arc in such a condition, that the revenues arc insufficient for covering expenses, would de facto amouut to the the introduction of a new and very extensive taxation, which predominant considerations would probably render inadvisable. þÿ According to the principles hitherto followed in these islands, the means required for covering the communal expenses have been always procured by taxes imposed by law This is the only system of taxation hitherto known, and it would hardly be advisable to deviate from it, the more so, as it has not been proved,

that such a measure has become necessary ; to the contrary, as far as Council arc aware, a balance of tho revenues and expenditure of the Land-treasury þÿ at least as far as regards St. Croix and St . CHOLERA, that dreadful scourge of the human race, is again in our neighborhood ; and it becomes us to take whatever steps lie in the power of weak mortals to prevent its visitation; or, if it should please the Almighty, in his wisdom, to afflict us, in such case to lessen at least its dreadful ravages. Oovernnv'nt, we understand, has given orders to the þÿl olicemasters to enforce strict sanitary regulations. We confidently hope, that the Pol.cemasters will, as formerly, devide the towns into districts; and assign each district to two or more inhabitants who shall examine every yard and report on the slightest cause of complaint. Our chief source of miasma, is the decomposing vegetable and other matters, deposited during rains, in the holes and hollows in our gutters, occasioned by their broken condition. There is for instance, a gutter in Queens Street, which has been for many years, nothing loss than a mudpool, showing ail the signs of active decomposition. For some years since, we understand, that it was in contemplation to repair the gutters; but the usual cry ot No means! No means! put a stop to tin' project. Now we must possitivelv declare, that an expense of six or seven hundred dollars should be no object, where the health, nay, the very existence, in a measure, of a community is imperiled ; and we are, from the necessity of the case, bold enough to urge, that steps be at once taken to effect the necessary repairs, in order that our gutters should be, what they arc in-
tended to he, þÿ drains þÿ and not mere reservoirs for the accumulation of filth.

( From the Journal of Commerce. ) As there are, from time to time, convulsions in Nature which are attended with beneficial results, so would it seem that the occasional civil upheavings and disruptions of communities are intended to work out beneficial results for the world at large. The disturbed state of the densely populated Chinese Empire, which has now prevailed for some time, is bringing about results which it would have been impossible to carry out some years ago. We have lately seen that foreign steam-vessels have been permitted to traverse its interior waters, unmolested, for a considerable distance ; and the people, who a few years ago it was difficult to draw, by any inducement.

from their own shores are, now voluntarily scattering themselves over the (ace of the globe, and becoming useful labourers and servants in different quarters. Chinese Emigration is now becoming the rule rather than the exception ; and, instead of looking distrustfully upon parties making agreements for service with them, the Chinese are now gladly emigrating, with their wives and families, to any country which offers the greatest prospect of peaceful residence, and some remunerative return for that ploddir.g industry winch has always characterised this singular people. The proximity of Siam, the þÿStraits Settlement, and the Islands of the Eastern Archipelago, has naturally drawn many of them to those localities to seek their fortunes, and there the number has always been considerable; hut it is only very recently that they have had courage to face, in large bodies, the lengthened voyage to (he West Indies and to the shores of Western America. In Penang there are about 17,000 Chinese engaged in various pursuits, hut principally agricultural. In Singapore and Malacca there are at least 100,000 Chinese. In the last five years more than 54,000 landed at Singapore; the number of junks touching at the Island being about 10,000 per annum. In California there are now over 20,000 Chinese ; and they are still arriving at San Francisco in shoals, some vessels being so crammed as to bring over 2,000 souls. They scatter themselves freely wherever they can obtain employment. At the Cliincha

Islands they are engaged in loading guano. On the works of the Panama Railway there are about 1 ,000 employed, at four dollars per month and their food ; and, as their engagements expire, the Planters ot Jamaica are hut too ready to secure them :it remunerative wages ii bounty of Cxi. per head being given by the Island Government for their introduction. They are described as intelligent and physically powerful men, anxiously disposed to engage in agricultural labour. Their intercourse with Europeans in various quarters cannot fail to he attended with beneficial results. Those who return to their country will be imbued with more correct notions of the þÿ barbarians than they have heretofore entertained; they will have learnt much ot our habits and customs þÿ of our progress ia the arts and sciences þÿ and of the articles most in request amongst us; and they will also have learnt to place some reliance on the faith of our engagements, the kindness of our treatment ot them, and the' stringency of our laws for the equal protection of all classes. In view of 1 lit extensive Emigration, which is now in operation in the Chinese ports, it behoves Rritish and Foreign Consuls to look to the comfort and health of the Emigrants, who, from being densely packed in native craft on long voyages, with insufficient food and water, experience a frightful mortality on the voyage. No such fears need he entertained as regards their voyage in Rritish ships where the regulations, as to provisions, space, and me-

dic\l attendance are more peremptory. This Chinese passengers-fralHic to various quarters bids fair to he a very important one. Those who have had the best opportunities of experience give a high character to the Chinese labourer for enterprise, energy, sobriety, intelligence, application, physical power, determined perseverance, cheerfulness, and prudent economy combined. Unfortunately and unfavourable impression lias been formed of them in some quarters from the fact that those who have been heretofore engaged have been the indolent lit-

toral population þÿ t he scum and out-cast of society, and a very unfair sample of tlie bulk of the population. In the Australian Colonies, especially as shepherds and herdsmen, in New South Wales and the northern districts þÿ in South Australia, Van þÿDiemen Land, s and New Zealand þÿ they would meet the pressing wants of the Colonists. In tropical regions they are equally effective, and infinitely preferable to the Coolies, who have been heretofore introduced. The Chinese labourers would by their enterprising and untiring industry, support themselves in comfort, and tend to raise our West India Colonies again to prosperity. Thousands of Chinese would, it appears, gladly exchange a life of comparative destitution anil starvation for abundance and comfort, and would willingly repay the cost of their transit by monthly instalments, as they already do, in the þÿStraits Settlements, advances of this kind made to them for passages and necessaries. The contracts of servitude should not he too long, and probably the cheapest way of obtaining the Chinese would be by vessels to the Isthmus of Panama. We find, then, that Chinese Emigrants have found their way in great numbers, and at their own expense, to Siam, Borneo, the Philippine Islands, Moluccas, Java, Singapore, Malacca, Penang, Madras, Calcutta, Bombay, Mauritius, California, Port Philip and to the Islands of Bally and Lombock, situated a short distance from the Australian Continent. In Singapore they form the bulk of the

labouring population, and arc, with few exceptions, the only dealers and cultivators of the soil. In Borneo, in the very teeth of its hostile inhabitants, they have formed flourishing Settlements. At Batavia they form a large and industrious portion of the population; the same al Manila. Thousands exist uiidei British rule at I long Kong, where all the public and private works are carried on by them. For all purposes þÿ agricultural, mechanical, nautical þÿ they seem available, and have greater powers of endurance and application than would seem to be indicated by their frame and stature. Witness the hard labour they perform loading guano at the Chinchas, and constructing the earthworks, &.C., on the Panama Railway- Our Merchants and Shipowners would do well to look more into this subject of Chinese Immigration, which, if properly conducted, would be attended alike with beneficial results to the Contractor, the Shipowner, the Planter, and the Labourers themselves. The high rates of Freight which have ruled so long, and the purposes of the war, have given hitherto full employment to our Mercantile Marine, but a return cargo of Chinese immigrants to the West Coast of America would often be most acceptable to ships which frequently proceed in ballast from Australia, and Eastern ports, to load guano in Peru. In his own country, the pay of a Chinese labonrci averages from Id. to (Id. a day, and on this stipend he contrives to maintain himself, together with Ins wife and

family þÿ his habits bein ' frugal, and Ins wants few. We are informed that, with the prospect of bettering their condition, any number of Chinese labourers and mechanics, of every description, might he easily induced to emigrate ; and we know that, when the advantages of a country become known to them, multitudes, at their own expense, find their way thither, as in the cases of Singapore and California.

sanguin ary struggle and glorious VICTORY. BATTLE OF IN KERMAN.

This important battle between the new ariivals of General 1 þÿlannenberg Corps s from Oiiessa and t he allies look place on Sunday, t he oil) of November, and lias been generally known as the battle of Sebastopol. Ii is now more correctly called Ihc bailie <>f lnkerman, Irom t be ruins of lnkerman close by. It was a bloody battle, as is generally the case win n the numbers are very disproporlioned, and the victory rests with the smaller army. Lord Raglan computes the Russian army to have amounted lo nearly HO 000 men. Prince McnschikolPs despaich says 40.000, bui, although that þÿgeneial r s eports have been more truthful of late, we may presume that the number is kept under, ns a defeat had to lie glossed over. General Cnmobcrl says 45 000. The number of our army engaged was 8,000 only, who resisted the whole Russian attack tor Hvo hours, when they were supported by 0,000 French, under General Bosquet, and at half-past one the enemy were driven off with a loss of 15,000, according to Lord Unglnn, and he is not given to exaggeration; of bom 8,000 to 10 (.00, according lo General Cnnrohert ; and of neatly !) 000, according to the Russian accounis General Dannenbcrg. who commanded Ihc Russians, had two horses killed under him, and all bin .Stall were wounded Forty-two officers including a general (Soimonoff), were killed, and two generals and 198 officers were wounded. The total loss has already been stated . Our loss has been three generals killed and four wounded: with 40 officers, 32 sergeants. 4

drummers, and 383 rank anil file killed, and 100 officers, 122 sergeants, 17 drummers, and 1,710 rank and file wounded! Our total of killed, wounded, amt missing is 2 012 Menschiknfl attributes their defeat to our siege artillery being turned upon them (we had only two guns), and the deadly flic of our Rifles. The Grand Dukes Nicholas Nicholaievile.h and Michael Nieholaievitch were with the Russian army. DETAILS FOUGHT ON THE FIFTH OF NOVEMBER We have again had a pitched battle with From the Morning Herald OF LNKERMAN, OF British Gamp. Nov. 7. THE BATTLE . the Russians þÿ a battle which, for duration

and loss of life, is only to he equalled by the tremendous conflicts of Bonaparte at Austerlitz and Leipsic In a word, t tie enemy, with an overpowering force, attacked the right of our entrenched camp at day-break on the morning of Sunday, the 5th of Nov. Their immense superiority of numbers enabled them to carry several strong positions, and penetrate into the centre of the camps of the Light and Second Divisions; but the opportune arrival of reinforcements enabled the allies to recover their lost ground, and eventually repulse the attack with such loss to the enemy as is, perhaps, unparelleled in the history of modern warfare. The English have lost no fewer than seven general officers killed and wounded, an unusually large proportion of other officers, and about 2,400 men. The French, who reinforced us. and turned the fortune of the day, have lost, asat Alma, about 1,400. Thelossof the enemy is lilerallv appalling. No words can convey an idea of the manner in which they have been slaughtered. Between 15,000 and 20,000 of their dead remain upon the field, in some places three and four deep. While the battle was raging on the right, a sortie was made from Sebastopol on the left of the French line. It was repulsed after a sanguinary engagement, in which our allies lost about 1.000 killed and wounded, and the Russians nearly 3,000. The fighting lasted about eight hours. The general officers whom we have lost are Lieutenant-General Cathcart, of the Fourth Division; Major-General Strangways, of the

Artillery ; and Brigadier-General Goldie, of the 2d brigade of the Fourth Division, all killed in action. The wounded are Lieutenant-General Sir George Brown, in the arm, slightly; his Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge, in the leg, slightly; Brigadier- General Torrens, a flesh wound ; and Brigadier-General Bentinck, a flesh wound. þÿ Ibid,

MISCELLANEOUS DETAILS. Kussiin Mine OiaeovEiiEii The French had carried a mine towards the main fortifications, and discovered a strong Russian mine, intended to blow up the French breaching battery. The French then countermined, and removed 1,900 cwt. of powder from the Russian mine. Scarcely a house in Sebastopol has escaped shot and shell.

A young Russian cadet, taken prisoner, said, that had we gone into Sebastopol after the battle of the Alma, we should have found opposed to us only two thousand men in the town, and eighteen guns in position ; now they have large numbers þÿ they go so far as to say three corps þÿd armee in the Crimea, and 500 guns in position in the town. Not only arc their batteries well filled, but every street is barricaded, and behind each barricade there are two or three guns

The French loss arose chiefly from the sot tie mnde by the garrison on their left. They drove them back with great loss, but following too far, exposed themselves to the fire of the batteries. Their total loss is about 1,400 killed nod wounded.

A committee ol inquiry (according to a correspondent) has been established, to ascertain the conduct of the Russians to our wounded. According to all accounts, their behaviour was barbarous. Many of our wounded were bayoneted on the ground.

For every Englishman or Frenchman dead on the field, there were eight or ten Russians. The wounds were frightful þÿ some were tipped open by shot or shell þÿ some had their legs blown oft þÿ others were headless, and the brains of many had actually dripped out of the immense holes made by the Millie bullets, leaving the skull empty.

A peculiar rifle bullet was much used bv, the enemy. A hole is groved out in Ihc flat side of the bullet ; this is filled with peicussion powder, causing it to burst like a shell on striking the object.

3 The English appear to have been taken completely by surprise (says a French writer) in the sortie made by the enemy upon their trenches on the 5th. The Russians had got possession of No. 1 and 3 Batteries, and spiked the guns before the French were in n condition to oppose them They were then attacked, and, after an obstinate defence, driven off with much slaughter. The French followed up their victory into the centre of the town, but having no reserve, and not knowing the result of the attack on out lines, they retired again.

The troops are prepating huts for the win ter, and are hourly expecting the arrival of reinforcements. The French say that they could take the town by three ways at any time they chose, but that it would be almost impossible to retain their position in the present reduced slate of the forces.

The writer was telling a French officer that the conduct of his men was the theme of our soldiers' enthusiastic praises They had not only been signalising themselves by their gallantry in the field, and by the admirable manner in which they had been handled, tint they had outshone all by the kindness, courte sy, and attention to our wounded in i lie evening. The French officer's reply was, Ah, but your men stood like a wall and, tinning to his neighbour, he paid us the compliment, þÿ was, It perhaps, as well that the English had to bear the first shock." There can be no doubt that the liussians poured three torrents of men upon us, and that it was a desperate attempt bv the airnv which had reached there but the day before from Odessa or the Danube, and commanded by the grand Duke Nicholas, to ntise the siege. Lord Raglan considered himself attacked by 60,000 men.

The liussians behaved with barbarous crucllv to our wounded ; every billon man was bayoneted. One English officer was wounded slightly, but unable to leave the spot with his men, as they retiicd fi r a while overwhelmed. When our troops recovered the ground, they found the pom fellow stabbed all over and stripped ! One Russian officer was seen to halt and limp about the field ; he had been wounded, Inn he loo was stabbing the fallen with his sword ! An orderly of the Duke of Cambridge went up to him and took him prisoner, and his royal highness was heard to promise the wretch that lie would do bis best to have him shot for Ins inhumanity. It is feared that this Russian barbarity provoked our men to give no quait er. They would throw down their arms, and, calling themselves Christians, beg for merry ; nnd if they were spared they would lake up their muskets and shoot ilieir preservers The French Zouaves also t ok no prisoners.

We h ave been politely favored with the perusal of a letter received by a Merchant in this City from his correspondent at St. Kitts, which gives a detailed account of the insidious destroyer Cholera. Want of room prevents our availing ourselves of the privilege accorded to us of extracting the entire contents of the communication ; we gather from it however that in spite of all sanitary measures, the average of mortality from its first appearance lias been from 8 to 15 per diem, anil that it was introduced into the colony by a young man who was landed from the last English Steamer, who reports that he came from a locality in London where it was awfully prevalent, and also states that lie had premonitory symptoms on board of the Steamer; and further that a death from Cholera had taken place on hoard. The disease had manifested itself with distressing virulence, as almost every case had proved fatal, thereby inducing the belief among the population that the medicines administered but enhanced their sufferings. The iron of the cylinder portion is half an inch thick, and the hermetical covers one and seven-eights inch thick. ©OO þÿe Preserved Meats. þÿ In consequence of the war in the East, and the difficulty of obtaining good supplies of animal food, several experiments have been made in Paris tor improving the mode of preserving meat. A nephew of M. Payne, the celebrated chemist, has submitted to the Government some dried meat, hut it was objected to by the War Department. The Minister of War is now trying some remarkable specimens

supplied by M. M. Delabarre and Bonnet. Their meat, dried nearly five months ago, lias resisted all the changes of dump and heat to which it has been subjected. It is dried by natural means; and in preparing it nothing is used that is not furnished by The animal itself. When (lie water which forms so large a proportion of the component parts of fresh meat is removed, a varnish composed of the pure osma/.ome of the animal is applied, and this, entering the pores, augments the nutritious properties of the meat, which has undergone no process of cooking, or been exposed to artificial heat of any kind, and, covering the surface, the meat is protected alike from damp or heat, and exposure to the air produces no effect upon it. The meat, although raw, may he oaten in that state, and is highly agreeable to the taste. It is reduced by desiccation one half, so that half the expense of carriage is saved; but when it lias to be cooked it is just put for about half an hour into warm water. It then recovers nearly its original volume, ai d, when cooked, cannot he distinguished from fresh meat which has just been supplied by a butcher. A still more extraordinary discovery is spoken of. It is said that a gentleman in one of the provincial towns of France has discovered the means of preserving for several months meat, fruits, Ac., without in any manner reducing them in size, flavour, or appearance. A leg of mutton, or a piece of beef, at the end of six or eight months or more, it is asserted, retains its origi-

nal appearance and all its original qualities. One of the most eminent scientific men in Paris stated that he saw and tasted strawberries gathered two months ago. and that they were just the same in flavour and appearance as if they had been gathered one half an hour.

From the Observer, December 3. 1854. THE BATTLE EVE IN THE RUS- SIAN CAMP. A correspondent of La Presse communicates the following curious information respecting the proceedings in Sebastopol and the Russian camp, from the arrival of the reinforcements under General Dannenberg till the battle of Inkerman þÿs þÿ The new reinforcements which have come lo the assistance of the Russians had been already announced to the commander-in-chief from Perekop. It was known that this army, commanded by General Dannenberg þÿ ihe most able, we þÿ are assured, of all the Russian generals and by two Archdukes Michael and Nicholas, was composed of the 10th, lltli, and 12th divisions. Each of these corps consists of 10 battalions of infantry, of two batteries of artillery, and of a force of cavalry, the number of which is rot accurately known. Altogether 30.000 men have arrived at Sebastopol, post haste, having left their baggage behind at Nicolaieff þÿ Having reached a forest, two leagues to the north-east of Sebastopol, the army halted, and the two archdukes put themselvesin communication with Prince Menschikoflf, who paid them a visit. A council of war was held on the 3d, at which the two archdukes, Prince Menschikoff and General Gortschukoff, were the only persons present. It was decided at the council that an attack should be made upon the allied forces two days afterwards. The army was to advance towards Inkerman to take possession of the fortified works which crown the heights and surround the plain of Inker man. After having accomplished this, I

the army was to attack the eastern side of the French works towards Balaklava. þÿ At the same time a vigorous sortie was to he made to help these operations. The point chosen was a spot hetwee.i the Port Quarantine and the Southern Fort. A portion of the garrison of the city and of the Southern port was to attack and destroy the first and second French batteries, which are causing considerable damage in the town. Menschikoff reserved to himself the I Crimea : þÿ þÿ Matters being thus arranged, Prince command of the town and the disposition of the columns which were to make the sortie. The army and the reinforcements which had come up were placed under the command of General Gort- 8chakoff. The army of operation was to receive also draughts of troops from the garrison of Sebastopol. The archdukes were placed on the staff. þÿ Measures were taken to ensure the due execution of these plans.

| þÿ On the 4th a solemn celebration took place. A mass was chanted with all solemnity by bishops who had come with the archdukes. At the end of the mass the troops were assembled, and one of the prelates addressed them. I should have been incredulous as to the details which I am about to communicate, had I not received them from a Russian officer, at present a prisoner at Balaklava, and if they had not been confirmed by special investigations which I have made for the purpose of ascertaining þÿ their truth. The bishop began by reminding the soldiers of their duty to the Czar and their country, and drew their attention to the two archdukes, who had corne to share their dangers. He then spoke of their enemies, and gave an explanation of the battle of Alma calculated to flatter the self-love and to elevate the courage of the imperial army. The English came under the special notice of the bishop. He said they were poor soldiers, destitute of all energy, and hostile to the cause of God. His allusions to the French were a mere echo of the proclamation of the Czar at Moscow in the year 1812. The most remarkable point, however, was the strange conclusion of the address. þÿ þÿ þÿ If you arc þÿconquerors, cried the bishop, þÿ greatjoy is in preparation for þÿyou. We know from unimpeachable sources that these English heretics have in their camp an enormous sum. which God will give into your hands. This sum amounts to thirty million roubles. The Emperor makes you a present of the third part of this tremen-

dous sum. The second third is reserved for the purpose of the re-building of Sebastopol, which you are on the point of relieving. The remainder will he divided amongst the princes and officers who will to-morrow he your commanders in the battle. Every one of you soldiers will receive 580 roubles. To the wounded the Emperor promises a þÿmonth pay s and rations. As to those of you chosen by God for a glorious death, your Emperor will permit you to dispose of your share in the booty by will. Whatever may he the wishes of any one of you, they þÿ will he þÿrespected. The speech was terminated by an appeal to the God of armies to bless the soldiers of Russia. A distribution of medals and coronets followed. þÿ The officer who has given me these curious details is a person of high family, with a spice of Voltairianism in his composition ; but he assures me that the scene was almost sublime. It was calculated to make a great impression on the soldiers, on whom Ihe recollection of the battle of Alma had operated most prejudicially. Whatever may have been the cause, whether it were the exhortation of the bishops, the presence of the princes, greed for gold, or any other reason, there is no doubt that the Russians fought most admirably on the morrow."
THE FRENCH EMPEROR AND THE FRENCH ARMY IN THE CRIMEA. The Moniteur publishes the following from the Emperor Louis Napoleon to General Canrobert commanding in the

þÿ Palace of St. Cloud, Nov. 24. þÿ General: Your report respecting the victory of Inkerman has excited deep emotion in my mind. Express in my name, to the army my entire satisfaction with the courage it has displayedwitli its energy in supporting fatigues and privations, and its warm cordiality towards our allies. Thank the generals, the officers, and the soldiers for their valiant conduct. Tell them that I warm-

ly sympathise with their misfortunes and the cruel losses they have experienced, and that my constant solicitude shall he directed to the task of softening þÿ lie bitterness of them. After the brilliant victory of the Alma, I had hoped for a moment that the routed army of the enemy would not so easily have repaired its losses, and that Sebastopol Would soon have fallen under our attacks; but the obstinate defence of that town and the reinforcements received by the Russian army have for the moment arrested the course of our success. I approve of the resistance you made to the impatience of the troops who wished to make the j No. 61, Harbinger; No. 81, Georgiantt. assault under circumstances which would have entailed too considerable losses. þÿ The English and French Governments direct their serious attention to their army in the East. Already steamboats are traversing the seas with considerable reinforcements. This increase of assistance will double your forces, and enable you to assume the offensive. A powerful diversion is about to take place in Bessarabia, and I receive the assurance that from day today in foreign countries public opinion becomes more and more favourable to us. If Europe should have seen without alarm our eagles, so long banished, displayed with so much cchtl, it is because it knows that we are only fighting for independence. If France has resumed the position to which she is entitled, and if victory has again attended upon þÿ declare it with pride to the patriotism her flags, it is þÿ I

and to the indomitable bravery of the army that I owe it. þÿ I semi (Jeneral de Montebello, one of my aides-de-camp, to convey to the army the rewards which it has so well merited. In the meantime, General, l pray God to have you in his holy keepþÿing. þÿ Ibid.

Communication. Mr. Editor ! In municipal regulations for towns, it has ever been deemed of vital importance that such sanitary measures he enjoined and enforced, as may best promote the comfort and health ot the residents; is it not therefore most strange that, whilst the rural population are admonished to keep a certain space around eacli dwelling neat and trim, to the exclusion of sties and their inmates, our towns continue to be infested witli hogs and goats, nay! their keeping sanctioned under the sole liability of being killed it found at large? Devoid of all fear of such ulterior measures being adopted, grunters and gruntlings arc consequently on their preambulations, at night; þÿ and ewes, their kills, and bearded sire frisk about in wanton dalliance within the purlieus of the town. Recalling to mind the former most unseemly manner of killing these animals and dogs in the public streets, I impute no blame to the police of holding the penalty in abeyance, besides which this body lias had very important matter to attend to since 1848, and the apprehensions it created are by no means as effective as of yore Again, the purveyors of veal, mutton, and pork slaughter their calves, sheep, goats, and hogs, some in the very heart of the town, all, wheresoever domiciled; and not a few have oft 6 to 8 of these amffials within their premises, and however careful they assert themselves to he in the cleansing of their homesteads, the effluvia and exhalations thence arising are by no means pleasant,

or sweet-smelling to those who live in their immediate neighborhood, and cerles, not salutary ; as they are also in t he habit of nailing against their houses, for drying, the skins of goats and sheep. I believe myself safe in asserting that, in the towns of most of the Westindia Islands, these nuisances are not tolerated and the keeping þÿ of hogs and goats is expressly prohibited in the town of St. Thomas þÿ and why not here? Experience, elsewhere, has fearfully taught, that pestilential diseases have always originated where the laws of

cleanliness have been utterly disregarded, and generally in certain localities of towns: must we not therefore rationally expect, if we thus continue to foster the elements of disease, that its natural sequence will as assuredly follow, as that thunder succeeds its premonitory flash? In the prohibiting of these animals being kept in town, let us not be lead to suppose that we are despoiling the poor of a means of livelihood, for the owners of such are mostly the indolent and t he idle, who keep them as a means of preventing the necessity of more strenuous exertion þÿ the truly poor keep none þÿ and if we continue to sanction the continuance of this practice, what are we, but the incipient promoters of that inert ion and idleness that leadetli to vagrancy, which the vagrant law so zealously strives to annihilate. What a nuisance hogs are, in another respect, the entrances to the town ot Christianstcd afford ample evidence, where the sides of the public road are ploughed and furrowed to the great annoyance of him who lias to repair them. T. 28th December 1854.

From the St. Thomas Times, December 20. COMMUNICATION. IMililic Examination of the Pupils attached to the þÿ Institution Cadillac. þÿ The 8th Annual Examination of t he Pupils of the þÿ Institution þÿCadillac commenced on Sunday at the local of the Institution, and terminated on Monday. The exercises comprised classifications of instructions in the different languages : þÿ French, English and Spanish, namely, exercises in Heading, Calligraphy, Analysis of Grammar in the different Languages, Geography, Deleniation of Maps, Arithmetic, Ancient and Modern History, Classical Recitations, Declamations &c., &,c. The Pupils of this valuable Establishment whilst exposed to the strictest scrutiny in various departments of excellent instruction in the French, English and Spanish Languages, have, as usual, maintained the respectable character of the Institution, and their individual claim to the admiration, esteem and love of the spectators, friends and relatives; these results are undoubtedly gratifying to every one who appreciates the elements which Education contributes to the social fabric, þÿ the public peace and order ! It would be superfluous, on our part, nor to would in this limited space attempt offer the we tribute to the worthy men, whose labours have long ere this obtained the unqualified approbation and support of the public here as well as beyond 1 he limits of the Island. We cannot however refrain to remark that the valuable exertions of Mr. Cadillac, supported by the zealous co-operations of Professors, judiciously

selected for the task, have proved the means of moulding to maturity and perfection the native intelligence of a large number of our youthful and interesting longing population, as well as many youths to the neighbouring Islands. be- þÿ Pupils distinguished for their moral qualifications, competent, annually sent forth to grapple with mental energy and resources, the career of life prescribed by their parents, Friends or fortune ! such have been and remain the object, the system of the þÿ Institution þÿCadillac! This system could not be overlooked colonies by men of þÿ ! intelligence in this, or other Men who understand, that a Statue lies hid in a block of Marble, and the art of the Statuary only clears away the superfluous matter and removes the

Rubbish. The figure is in the stone, and the sculptor only finds it. What sculpture is to a block of marble, Education is to the human Soul. The Philosopher; the Saint; or the Hero; the Wise, the Good, or the Great man; very often lies hid and concealed in a Pleibean which a proper Education might have dis-interred, and brought to light. Hence the number of Pupils who have completed their education at this Academy ; who have retired abroad, or remain in this Community are brilliant illustrations as well as flattering testimonials to the character of our Colony. We cheerfully subscribe to the merits of the Institution either locally or its relative importance considering our foreign relations ; such impressions extend far and wide; it could not be otherwise! þÿ Organized on a liberal scale ; without any considerations of economy ; unmindful of the outlay in regard to- the supply of competent Teachers, and possessing all the means indis-

every inducement is thus offered to Parents, and an enlightened Public to bestow the manifold advantages of Education without incurring the danger and risk of sending their Children many thousand miles across the faithless Atlantic besides tbe pangs of separation. The varied incidents connected with the examination, which form the subject of this article, establish the efficiency of the Personel under which the Establishment is conducted, and we take pleasure in introducing the names of parties who, according to the public estimation of professional merit, are worthy of liberal consideration and public patronage. From the Observer, December 3. 1854. THE B\LTlC--STATE OF AFFAIRS. Collets fiom Riga of the 16ih stale that the English flying squadron, which, alter the departure ol t lie allied fleets, remained in observation in ihe ilallic, had been reinforced, and that it then consisted of twelve vessels. The excursion of the Russian war steamers 1mm Sweaborg and Revel rendered those reinforcements indispensable to enable the English cruisers to cope with the Russians should the latter advance into the Baltic. The English steam corvette Archer entered Memel on the 21st. but only remained there the time necessary to deliver despatches for Government to the British Consul. She afterwards joined the flying squadron, which lately captured a number of Finnish vessels, laden with salt and colonial goods. This year the number of vessels belonging to the maritime nations which passed the Sound was by 5,000 inferior to that of last year. The number of English vessels which sailed through that passage in 1853 amounted to 4,683, while this year it did not exceed 2 000. The Danish Government, which levies a toll on all vessels passing through the Sound, was thus deprived of the principal financial resources of the kingdom. The two younger sons of the Czar are not expected for some time to return to St. Petersburg. The passage of Russian reinfoicements for the Crimea continued without interruption. Most of the generals who held commands during tbe war in Finland, and in the towns bordering on the Gulf, have successively repaired

to the capital, in order to be employed in the active armies. General Rokassowski, Commander-in-Chief of the troops in Finland, had also arrived at St. Petersburg, as well as General Owander. chief of the Third Division of Infantry of the Imperial Guard. It appears positive the! all danger of an attack

A þÿ Protest from the passengers of the Royal Mail Steamer þÿParana is inserted in the St. Thomas Times of the 27th December last and copied in this paper. It is certainly a very unpleasant affair ; but who is the blame ? 'The Mil itary, stationed at t he W estern Fort in St Thomas, in obedience to the Port Regulations fired first a blank shot and afterwards sharp shots at the vessel, because she was not provide rl with a night pass, which the captain or consignees, when clearing her out, neglected to procure. By accounts, she received some injury, which we hope, is very trilling. It is, however, our firm conviction that the matter will he satisfactorily arranged by both Governments, and that more precaution will in future he observed.

On hoard the Benjamin Franklin ) otF St. Thomas, 22ml Deer., 1854. þÿSIR, We the undersigned passengers by the Royal Mail Steam þÿCompany s Packet Parana, from England to St. Thomas, but transhipped at this latter place to the American Steamer Benjamin Franklin, in consequence of the English intercolonial Steamers having left St. Thomas previously to the arrival of the Parana, beg to represent to you as acting British Consul that a most flagrant and atrocious outrage was perpetrated yesterday evening by the Danish Authorities in command of the Western Fort
gers on hoard the Benjamin Franklin, by their firing three shotted guns at her, to
convenience and detriment both of the Passengers and of Her Britannic Majes-

3 þÿty s Mail Service by the Steamer being obliged to put back into port to repair tile damage caused by the finrig of the Fort, before she could safely proceed on her outward voyage. We beg to point out most strongly that this wanton and unprovoked aggression took place under circumstances of peculiar aggravation, and in defiance of all recognized usages of the civilized world. The Benjamin Franklin had been hailed from the Western Fort in passing and her Captain had stated the þÿShip name, s and the service she was proceeding upon, although it is probable that as he did not understand the language (supposed to he Danish) addressed to him from the Fort by the Authorities there, they might not have understood what was said by him in return in English. A blank shot was then fired from the Fort as a signal to the Steamer to stop ; this signal was obeyed, but notwithstanding a shotted gun was soon afterwards fired directly at the vessel, and struck her on the main wale on the starboard quarter '? The Captain of the Steamer then reversed his engines, and backed the vessel toward the Fort, but no notice was taken either of her stopping or returning to port , ami two other shotted guns were fired at her in rapid succession, but providentially without doing any further injury! A boat was now immediately lowered ,'om the Steamer, and three of the English passengers (the Lieut.- -Governor of St. Vincent and his Private Secretary, and the Bishop of Guiana) proceeded direct to the Fort to ascertain the cause

of so unparalleled an outrage, and to stop any further firing; upon arrival at the Fort, it was found that no Danish officer was present there, and all that could be learnt was that the Benjamin Franklin had been fired at because she was not provided with a night pass ! As it appeared far from improbable t hat in I lie absence ofany proper or intelaggression might lake place, the Lieut. - ligent authority at the Fort some further G< vrrnor of St. Vincent and the Bishop of Guiana landed and remained there to prevent this, whilst the Lieut. -Goverþÿnor s Private Secretary was sent on in the boat accompanied by one. of the Danish soldiers, to the Town Fort, to seek for further explanation, and some clear order not to renew the firing. Upon that þÿgentleman s return he stated that he had seen the Officer in command of the Fort, and had been informed by him that the firing took place in consequence of the Benjamin Franklin not being provided with a night pass; that Officer had also expressed his regret at the occurrence, and stated that the vessel was at liberty to proceed þÿ but as it was necessary to return to port to repair the damage sustained, it was not possible to do this; and we, moreover, all feel that we owe it to ourselves, to our country, and to all future passengers (who, if a stop be not put to such outrageous proceedings, may hereafter be placed in the same imminent peril that we were), not lightly to pass over so serious and so aggravated an aggression, by which,

but for the merciful protection of a Divine Providence, many lives might have been lost, for there is no doubt but that if the gun from which the first shot was fired had been in the slightest degree more elevated, that shot must have swept through and cut down many of the crowd of passengers collected on deck just above where it struck, and a large number of whom were ladies. We beg to point out that the Benjamin Franklin had been chartered by he Royal Mail Steam Company to convey the Passengers and Mails from England to their respective destinations, not only

with the knowledge and sanction of the English and French Consuls, but with the express consent of the Danish Authorities, by whom the vessel was cleared at the Custom House, and whose duty it was to have sent an immediate notice to their Forts to permit her to pass: nor can we help remarking that even if as is stated the laws of the country required that the Captain should have been provided with a night pass to authorise his departure from port after dark, ice do not consider this as in the slighest degree lessening the outrage committed. We are informed, that all the Steamers carrying the English and Foreign mails are exempted from this regulation, but even were it not so, nothing could justify cowardly and murderous fire upon unarmed passengers, ladies and children, in a vessel close under the guns of the Fort, after that vessel had first stopped in her course , and afterwards reversed her engines and put back in obedience to a blank shot fired in the first instance ! ! We understand that the Lieutenant- Governor of St. Vincent will report the occurrence direct to the English Government ; hut we feel that we ought at the same time at once to call upon you, as the acting British Consul, to take immediate steps to demand explanation and reparation for the insult and injury to which we have been subjected, and for the interruption which has been occasioned to Her Britannic þÿMajesty Mail s Service, as well as to require that some satisfactory steps be taken to prevent in
