IIOW THE TELEGRAPH IS WORKED. Prince Mensclukoft is said lo have reported from Sebastopol, on the J9th hist , that the fire of the allies had been slackened for some days, and had almost entirely ceased on the 18th. The authority upon which this news rests is a telegraphic message, alleged to have been received at Berlin Itoni Warsaw, on Sunday lost. Now, with regard to the abstracts of Menschikofl despatches, transmitted by private telegraph, it is right that the public should, once for all, ho informed, that an extensive manufacture of them is carried on at Trieste. The raw material, worked up into these telegraphic messages.

is imporled for the most part from Odessa or Constantinople. The principal correspondents, or factors of the establishment, are Greek houses in Russia or the Levant, The messages are forwarded from Trieste lo Vienna, Berlin, Warsaw, and Paris, and reissued from these capitals, the Trieste matk having been effaced For the news they contain there is genet ally some foundation in tact ; hut, as it is originally picked up by eaves-dropping, the original is sadly travestied, owing to the dulness of perception, or mental stolidity, or partisan bias of the eavesdroppers. It is still further distorted in passing through t tie alembic of the Trieste inanufuciurer ; of whose wares the account ol a battle fought before Sebastopol on the 13th, gravely and credulously published by a contemporary on Saturday week, is a characteristic sample. '1' lie re are probably other manufactories of latest news from the seal of war, similar to that in Trieste ; but as yet they have not been detected. When so many counterfeit despatches are in circulation, it is unnecessary to add that they must be received with great caution. þÿ Observsr.

In justice to myself and for the satis faction of the public; as well as for the purpose of correcting an erroneous imputation which rumour is at present myself undeserving any busy with, 1 feel called upon to whatever blame declare for the apparant non-improvement ot the children belonging to the school in which I lately acted as under teacher. But rnmour says that I have been discharged on account of the late examination not proving satisfactory: there be-

ing no perceptible improvement in the children. So far as improvement is concerned, I cannot hot grant that rumour is in the right. But now for the cause. How can it be expected that any school can progress where there are no materials for carrying out plans and extending the instructions; and where the majority of the children attend so irregularly. On the other hand, to form a correct judgment of the progress of a school, in a greater or lesser degree, it is necessary first to have known the former state of that school, and in the second place to know whether those particular children attended regularly or not, how long they had been attending, and what tliey knew when they entered. That there is room for improvements in the upper as well as t lie lower school, and particularly in the lower is obvious. But is it the business of the lowest teacher to make those improvements ? Certainly not. The first or upper teacher whose business it is to know every particular connected with the schools, to form plans for their benefit, and to inspect regularly every department, knows, virtually, very little about the lower school, its plans or its progress. YYras it then my business to form plans and carry them out, or even to suggest them? This would have been acting out of my place. Consequently I stand acquitted and rumour is false. Again. Rumour asserts that the first or upper teacher, by some misrepresentations to my prejudice, to satisfy, as is conceived, some private pique, for which

/cannot account, lias been the primary cause of my dismissal. This however, cannot he true, since lie knows as little, I believe, about my character as a n an as he does of my abilities as a teacher, therefore it would have been most illiberal to vilify the former or censure the latter. The upper teacher never once even hinted to me that there was any lack of duty on my part or on the part of my superior in office, which gave me the assurance that lie was satisfied, under prevailing circumstances, that I did all that could be done under those circumstances. Yet I have been discharged and without there being any reason assigned, the substance of the communication from government being that my services were no longer required. As some opportunity may offer for me again to he employed in the business of teaching and as the rumour now afloat may then operate to my prejudice, I have taken this opportunity to make this public declaration. And I trust that those persons whose children have positively improved in comparison to the time they have attended, will do Mr. Beech and myself the justice to acknowledge it. YVest End January 2nd 1855. CHRISTIAN C. YVISI'ETALL.

THE FRENCH SOLDIER AND HIS EQUIPMENTS. The Constitutionel , in the course of an article in which it passes in review the material ameliorations introduced into the French army which were rendered necessary by the operations in Africa, and which have been found so advantageous in the East, says þÿ " Necessity is a good counsellor, and to it we owe the improvements in the equipment and manner of feeding the soldiers, which have produced such good results in the East, and which will produce important consequences if ever a conflict should break out in Europe. Experience has shown how strengthening food can he supplied with diminution of weight. During the expeditions biscuit was substituted for bread, rice was employed in rations, coffee was substituted for wine, and the biscuit broken into the coffee gave the soldier strength to support the most painful fatigues. Such was, with meat, the basis of food in Africa. The small volume occupied by it enabled six and even eight days' rations to he placed in the knapsacks, and that diminished the embarrassments ofthe baggage-train. Blankets were found to be only a slight protection against the pernicious effects of damp in the nights, and the hospitals were encumbered with patients labouring under ague, until tente-abri was discovered. That was almost the salvation of the army. The tente-abri is three feet high, four and a half long, and is composed of three pieces ofcanvass, attached by buttons or strings. Two sticks placed at each extremity serve to support it,

and it is fixed by wooden pins to the earth. Three minutes suffice to set it up, and two to take it down. Each tent accommodates three men ; each of the three carries a piece ofthe canvass, and they divide the sticks and pins among them, and so they march. The first thing they do on arriving is to fix the tent, and to dig a trench to carry off the water in case of rain. At night tlicy sleep wrapped in blankets, and with their knapsacks for pillows. They are thus preserved from damp or rain. The tente-abri permits an army always to bivouac in the open fields, and does away with the necessity of dividing it among different villages, so that it is always united. A guarantee for discipline, and a protection for health, it preserves the effective force, and assures the duration of an army. It is, without contradiction, one of the great benefits from Africa, and one of the things which will have the greatest influence on the state of our armies, whatever may be the field into which they may be called to combat. With his six days' provisions, his camping effects, his equipment, the piece of canvass for his tent, his blanket, and

THE NON SUBSCRIBER. The following amusing description of the blessed state of ignorance of a family who never took a newspaper, we extract from an American paper. We hope there are few families in our island in the sitme condition; if so, they had better take warning, and come and enrol their names at once, on the subscription list of our journal. The Man that don't take his country paper was in town yesterday. He brought the whole family in a two-horse waggon. He still believed that General know ' If the Kamschatkins' had taken Taylor was president, and wanted to Cuba, and, if so, where they had taken it. He had sold his corn for twenty five cts. the price being thirty-one, but upon going to deposit the money, they told him it was mostly counterfeit. The only hard money he had was some three ct. pieces, and these some sharper had 'run on him' for half dimes ! His old lady smoked a 'cob pipe,' and would not believe that anything else could be used. One of the boys went to a blacksmith's shop to be measured for a pair of shoes, and another mistook the market house for a church. After hanging his hat on a meat-hook, he piously took his seat on a butcher's stall, and listened to an auctioneer, whom he took to he the preacher. He left before the ' meeting was out' and had no great opinion ofthe 'sarniit.' One of the girls took a lot of seed onions to the post-office to trade them for a letter. She had a baby, which she carried in a 'sugar trough,' stopping at times to rock it on the side-walk.

When it cried, she stopped its mouth with an old stocking, and sang ' Barbary Allen.' The oldest boy had sold two 'coon-skins,' and was of a ' bust' þÿ when last seen he had called for a glass of ' sody and water,' and stood soaking gingerbread and making wry faces. Tile shop keeper mistaking his meaning, had given him a mixture of salsoda and water and it tasted strongly of soap. But ' he had heard tell of sody and water, and was bound to give it a fair trial puke or not puke. Some ' town fellow' came in and called for lemonade, with a 'fly in it,' whereupon our 'soaped' friend turned his back, and quickly wiped several flies into his drink. We approached the old gentleman, and tried to get him to subscribe, but lie would not listen to it. He was opposed to 'internal improvement,' and he thought 'larnin' was a wicked invention, and culterwaten' nothin' but Wanity and Wexafion.' None of his family ever learned to read but one boy, and he ' teached school awhile, and went a studyin' diwinity.' þÿ Antigua Weekly Times.

An American medical gentleman, who some years since visited Paris under circumstances favorable to his admission supporters of " The Empire tells a ca- to a circle of the survivors and former ," pital story, as he heard it related by the celebrated General Excelmans, one of Napoleon's " Paladins.'' It was at a dinner-party, composed of some of the survivors of Waterloo, a few of their younger relatives, and the action of an ex-king on a visit from his

home in America, and to whom the gentleman owed his introduction to the circle we have mentioned. Some question arose about bravery, when the younger members of the company were electrified to hear the venerable and heroic Excelmansgravely and seriously declare- " Men are all coicards in the dark !" The General smiled at their expression of dissent ; remarked that it was " very like youth ;" and proceeded to relate the following anecdote, in support of his strange declaration : There was a young hot-head in the Emperor's service, who,, burning for action, and his duties for the time affording no opportunity, at last resolved to fight a duel ; accordingly, choosing to construe some remark or other of an older and superior officer into an insult, he challenged him. The old soldier, waiving all considerationsof rank, agreed to meet the young man, but on the following unusual terms: The time should he night þÿ the place a þÿroom in opposite corners of which they were to stand. The seconds, having placed their men, were to withdraw outside of the door, taking the candles with them. The word should be given from without, when he who had the first fire should discharge his weapon, and the seconds having the light should immediately rush in. These strange conditions were accepted ; the time arrived; and the seconds placed the parties as agreed upon þÿ withdrawing immediately, and leaving their men in the dark. The word was given þÿ the fire was heard þÿ the door was re-opened þÿ and

there stood the elder of the two bolt upright in the corner, his adversary's ball having entered the wall so close to his head that his escape seemed little less than miraculous ! It was now the old soldier's turn to fire. They were again left in the dark ; the word was again given from the outside ; and instantaneously with the discharge the seconds rushed in to find the challenger prostrate upon the floor, not yet having recovered himself from his trick to avoid the ball, which, on examination, it was found must have killed him! The young man was covered with confusion, and the seconds were overwhelming him with the expression of their scorn, when the veteran stopped them. " Not so fast ! not so fast ! my young friends," said he; you will live to grow wiser. Where do you suppose 7 was at the first fire ? On my hands and knees in the corner ; but I was up quicker than lie. Ah ! Messieurs, say what we will þÿ boast as we may þÿ we arc all cowards in the dark /" It was afterward ascertained that the story was an actual fact, and that the elder of the parties was no other than the brave warrior Excelmans himself!

THE CASHIER AND HIS CHARM- ING CUSTOMER. When a cashier in a banking-house commits an error by paying too much, the loss falls upon the clerk, unless there he any extenuating circumstances to justify a contrary course; the mistake is then called a clerical error. Our readers will not be at a loss to know in which category to place the following. One Monday morning a very elegantly-dressed female entered the banking-house of and presented a check for payment, at the same time requesting, with a great show of politeness, that she might have gold in exchange for the check. The lady was not only well dressed, hut she" was very beautiful; so much so, that the attention of the cashier was riveted upon her. He weighed fifty sovereigns, which he handed to the lady; and supposing that she would count them one by one, he anticipated that the pleasure he enjoyed in looking upon her would thereby be prolonged ; but he was of mistaken ; for to his surprise, instead counting them, she huddled them all up together, and put tlieni in a white pocket handkerchief. The cashier, observing this unusual mode, said, 'You had better count them madam;' but the lady, looking at him with a most gracious smile, replied, 'I am quite satisfied, Sir, that you are right ;' and, with another bewitching look, wished him good-day, and walked leisurely out of the bank. the The beauty cashier of was bis so customer, overpowered im- that with mediately on her retiring he went a him paces to a fellow cashier and asked few

if he had ever seen such a lovely creature. he is too ! 'Such a bewitching woman!' said he ; ' what a sparkling brilliancy there was in her eyes! 1 wonder who she is?' This caused him to look at the check, which on first receiving he had placed on his book, without entering or once glancing at it ; when he that his utter astonishment discovered to £5 instead of £50. Uttering an exclamation, he jumped over the counter, and

to the right and to the left, but could distinguish no trace of the beautiful lady ; he ran in and out of the several courts that surrounded the bank in vain ; he returned to the banking-house to take counsel with his fellow admirer of this charming woman, as to the best course to adopt, when it was decided that he should immediately apply to the drawer of the check for the same and address of the party to whom he paid it, the body of payable to 'house expences or bearer ' the check simply expressing it to be The drawer of the check, on being asked by the cashier to furnish him with the desired information, expressed his surprise of what he called his impertinent curiosity ; but, on being informed of the mistake that had been made, he immediately gave the name and address, ' Miss Thompson, Bury Street, Saint James's; adding, I beg you will not utter a word of this affair to any one, for if it should come to the ears of Mrs. P I fear the most serious consequences would result from my indiscretion, for the party in question is; I fear, only too celebrated.' The cashier, anxious to catch the lady on her return home, assured the gentleman of his silence, and proceeded with the utmost expedition to Bury Street. The door was opened by an innocentlooking girl, who, on being asked if Miss Thompson was at home, replied with great simplicity, 'No, Sir, Miss Thump.son is not at home;' and as though she wished to stifle all further inquiries, she added, 'I don't think she will come back.'

It ultimately came out that, the moment ' Miss Thompson,' returned from the city, she packed up her things and left the house, of course without leaving her address or any clew to her whereabouts ; enjoying, no doubt, the satisfaction of having proved the truth of the saying that 'Love is blind' ; for she had by a judicious exercise of her charms so far blinded the eyes of a city banker that he could not distinguish between five and fifty pounds. This was a sad termination of the affair to the cashier, who on his return to the bank felt ashamed to mention the circumstance to the house, and it was arranged that the drawer of the chdck should, by way of purchasing the silence of the cashier, pay one half of the amount, and the cashier the other, which was done; and the affair was kept a profound secret for some time. þÿ St. Lucia Palladium.

Editor! 1 beg you will allow me to state, in the columns of your paper, a few words in defence of rational amusements, which it was my misfortune to hear very unwisely assailed a few evenings since. on Our Divine Maker lots bestowed Man a faculty, on which Phrenology has bestowed the name of Mirthfulness. This faculty gives a taste for, and causes us to relish, amusement. It can no more be extinguished than appetite ; because both are the product of an innate element in the mind. Ministers, in accordance with the Puritanical Dogma, that amusements were inherently sinful, have preached and prayed against them for these three hundred years, but without the least avail. In my opinion they may as well preach against a northwester. And will God regard their prayers when they pray him to suppress a faculty which He Awscreated ? No! These long faces may just as well join in and help direct publicamusement, because restrain them they cannot. Since men will "laugh and grow fat" all that religion can do is to furnish innocent amusements, and render them as useful as possible. "Within the mind" says the Rev. Henry Ward Beecher, of whom America is justly proud, in his lecture in favour

of amusements "there are faculties which answer to the flowers and the beauties of the natural world, such as mirthfulness, ideality, benevolence ; and in the development of these powers depends in a great degree the happiness of man." These are the words of one of the greatest Preachers of the Gospel in America ; and they will find an echo in the breast of every intelligent man, in spite of all Puritanical remarks made to the contrary. One man's Yes is as good as another man's No in the absence of proof. And I would take great interest in seeing it proved from the text of Holy Writ that we shall renounce all innocent and rational amusement. Eet us take care that in preventing such amusements, we do not encourage private and pernicious ones. The man, who, because he dissents on conscientious principles from amusements, brands the whole world as unchristian, because they do not see as he does, assumes too much. What right has one mortal to arraign another at the tribunal of his conscience, and there condemn him for what the conscience of the other acquits him. The religious world, it is well known, is not agreed on the principle assumed by some, that amusements are pernicious. What right then has the one party to sit in judgment on the other? No! Mr. Editor, I think a little more respect for the principles and opinions of others when they differ from our own, would be very advisable in certain places. God has bestowed on me the faculty of enjoying amusement ; and as long as

I do not abuse it, I scorn the man who would charge me with a violation of Christian Principles in obeying the dictates of that faculty. One of the forms of amusement, upon which so much abuse has been heaped is that of scenic representations: but even this, when under proper regula-

s & © i A yr i a, tions, might be made a perpetual source of the most noble and useful entertainments. As usually conducted in public, I will grant that a most powerful engine is made the subject of great abuse, and many instantly argue from the abuse against the use ; they seem determined to consider the whole machine as purely diabolical, even when employed as in the case in question, in a private house and for the private amusement of a few friends. But suppose the piece performed to have no tendency but by the most engaging means, to encourage and animate virtue and piety ; wh it would there then be in such an amusement to call down an Anathema? The beautiful remarks of Addison in the Spectator on the moral uses to which the stage is capable of being applied, are well known : and even Watts, whom no one will accuse of laxity of moral or spiritual principle, allows, that it is only the " abuse that makes the theatre an evil. A dramatic representation," he observes, "of the affairs of human life, is by no means sinful in itself: I am inclined to think, that valuable compositions might be made of this kind, such as might entertain a virtuous audience with delight, and even with some real profit. Such have been written in French." "Indeed," says another Divine "the drama was originally connected with religion : among the ancients, dramatic performances formed part of the solemnities of their religious festivals ; and on their revival in more modern times, the subjects of them were taken from the

scriptures, the theatre for performing was the church, and the performers the clergy." In the face of all this, I confess my esteem for the value of whatever instruction I might have received in certain quarters, to be considerably lessened when I hear it asserted " that we cannot worship God on Sunday when we witness a private stage performance on Saturday evening." To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir, Although the performance of the Amateurs last night was private, I would take the liberty through your paper to make a few remarks, hoping they will be taken in the same kind spirit they are meant. I beg leave first to express my great satisfaction at the success of the performance, in which satisfaction it appeared the whole audience partook, and Invitation, " to refrain from all expres- I am sure it was only the request in the sion of approval or disapproval" which prevented the audience applauding as the performance merited. Secondly, I would express the hope, that this performance be only a nucleus for greater attempts of the same kind, and that an association be formed for that purpose, and for defraying the expences connected therewith, as it could not be expected that such should solely be borne by the performers. Yours truly 7th January 1855.

They confirm the news that

The Majestic and Cressy, which sailed from Kiel on t lie 3rd , passed the Belt on the 5th, in charge of native pilots. The weather was calm hut hazy. The Vienna correspondent of the Chronicle states that Sebastopol is provisioned for not more than 14 to 16 weeks, and the Russian relieving army altogether depends for its support upon the supplies sent front Southern Russia. These are conveyed in all descriptions of vehicles, principally drawn by oxen, which tire as much exposed to destruction in the Tauridian steppes as the ships of the allies in the Black Sea. A correspondent of the Vienna Fremden Blett, it journal usually very favorable to Russia, adds that a train of several hundreds of wagons, laden with provisions and munitions for the Russian troops at Bakshiserni, was surprised by the frightful snow storms in the steppes south of Perekop and annihilated. Berlin, Dec. 3rd From exact information as to the losses sustained by the allied fleets it appeared that in the stor u of the 14th, 14 ships were wrecked near Sebastopol, and two ships of the line, two steamers, and 13 vessels of different classes driven on shore near Eupatoria."

From the London Morning Herald , Dec. 4. " Let bygones be bygones." There are two lights in which this remarkable appeal requires to be contemplated þÿ namely, the ineffable meanness of those who can make it a second time, and the equally ineffable folly which those who make it must attribute to the persons whom they think capable of being gulled by it. It is, in fact, an affront to the common sense of the nation, similar to that which we have before recorded in the complaint of an Irish alderman against a certain Lord Lieutenant of that country þÿ namely, that the "Viceroy insulted his intellect by the transparency of the untruths he told him." Lord Derby said þÿ and the sentiment represented þÿ was worthy of himself and the party he that " he would not be a Minister on sufferance." What are we to think of a Coalition which would persuade the nation to permit of their continuance in office out of contemptuous pity? The meanness of the appeal is patent. Let us come to the folly of those who could accede to it. Let bygones be bygones! What arc t hose bygones ? 1. A i attempt to prevent the possibility of the French alliance by gross abuse of the Emperor ami nation. 2. Credulity or connivance with regard to Russian aggressions. 3. A year and a half wasted in absurd, if not treacherous, negociations. 4. An army sent out without preparation as a demonstration. 5. An army left four months at Varna, to die of cholera. 6. An expedition sent to the Crimea, to gull Parliament, in the fall of the year,

when the winter was coming þÿ the force not being one-half the strength required to do the work. 7. An army left without any reinforcements till it is too late to send them for any other purpose than to save the lives of those who are compromised. 8. A war on which the liberties of Europe depend, starved to indulge a financial crotchet. 9. Permission to a false ally to destroy our own troops by paralysing the action of a sincere one. 10. Neglect to furnish our troops with hospital necessaries, or even surgeons, and leaving them till far into the winter without clothes and without proper food,

IT CJtO J ATI W- 11. Pushing the war into the winter, | and thereby losing in one gale of wind 32 transports, and damaging our menof-war. 12. These proceedings have cost us in all, 20,000 of the best soldiers of the world, and left us on the 1st December as far from our object, the taking of Sebastopol, as we were on the 1st of Sep. These are a few, and only a few of the bygones we are expected forget to þÿ and that without a single proof that Ministers even possess a determination to do better in future. Really, the Dublin alderman had not half as good cause of complaint the British public. as Fancy the howl of the Times had Lord " Derby's bygones bygones." Why, they Government made a plea of let be are not yet forgiven, and never will be, their conscientious opposition to the bubble of free trade, although eight years have elapsed ; and time, with wheat at 80s. a quarter, has proved that they were perfectly in the right. Our Ministry have i.ot even given up their crotchet of robbing Turkey to place the Principalities in the hands of the power which has directly caused all our losses in the Crimea. If they have, what means the ominous sentence wh'ch we quote from the Aberdeen organ ? " Better would it be for the Porte to " lose altogether provinces which it has " ceased to govern, and cannot afford to "defend, than to hold them by so prc- " carious a tenure." We said above that we were now as far from taking Sebastopol as we were on the 1st of September. We were wrong in so saying, for most assuredly

we are much further. At that time we had the game in our own hands. If we had sent a sufficient force þÿ nearly treble what wc did send þÿ and insisted upon Austria allowing Omar Pacha to act effectively on the Pruth, we might þÿ not as easily as the Times anticipated, however þÿ have planted our banners on its walls before Christmas. Having i cglectcd those commonsense precautions, þÿ mere "bygones," þÿ of course we have failed, and our army is besieged, while the lire against the city had stopped for three days at the date of the latest intelligence. The worst of all these " bygones" is that they are irreparable. We protest we have now our doubts as to whether we shall ever take Sebastopol at all ; and we believe that if we do so, it will be after many, many months of blockade, and not by active siege operations. The first process it appears which Ministers now contemplate is to leave our army to freeze through the long winter months upon the coldest and most exposed promontory in the proverbially "inhospitable" Euxine. Surely they do not expect that this force will be ready for active operations after such an exposure. If they should be so, they are the most extraordinary troops in the world, as remarkable for their powers of enduring hardships as they are for fighting. Now this, with all our admiration of them, we do not believe them to be. Well, let us suppose the long winter over, in What state will things be in the Crimea at the approach of spring? The Russian army, which will have

passed its winter in snug quarters at Simpheropol and Baktchi-Serai, will be reinforced probably to 200,000 men; for notwithstanding the assertions of the Times , travelling in winter after the frost sets in is easy in Russia transporting | with an assurance that if they admit the þÿ provisions still easier; and they will be well supplied with all necessary materiel and provisions, for, as has been well observed by a correspondent, we have over-

. looked the districts above Taganrog altogether as sources of supply. It is obvious that commencing the siege a second time, without investing the north side as well as the south, would be mere folly. We shall therefore have to fight a campaign in order to drive the relieving army out of the Crimea, before we can attempt even to commence our approaches. Well, 1 et us once more suppose the Crimea cleared of the enormous army which the Czar will have collected, the last Cossack driven beyond Perecop, the isthmus rendered unattackable as Kalafat, and that the allied army has returned to commence the siege. We can hardly conceive all this to be accomplished before the latter end of July or beginning of August. We shall then require for investment 10,000 men a mile, according to the Duke of Wellington ; at this rate, 13 miles þÿ at a calculation which even Mr. Gladstone could make þÿ gives us 130,000 men. Now, it must be remembered that as the harbor of Sebastopol cuts oft'the investing army from all power of assisting one wing by succours from another þÿ and, as the garrison þÿ say 40,000 men will occupy a central posi- þÿ tion, they can bring a preponderating force to bear upon any point of the circumference. Wc merely mention this as a fact, for we do not expect the Russians to make sorties. No, they will trust to their heavy artillery and formidable earthworks. We have proved to our cost what can be done in this way in a month; what may we not expect to find at the end of six or eight ?

As a specimen of the preparations making by the Czar, we quote a letter recently received from a friend at Berlin ; the writer is a Swede : þÿ " In a public-house (at Berlin), I met "six Englishmen. They had come through "Holland, en route to Russia, to supcrin- "tend the casting of long-range l/incas- "ter guns for Cronstadt. Thousands of "men are at work on all the Gulf ports." Now, it is hardly likely that Sebastopol will be neglected, or that some of the patriotic Englishmen in question will not be sent to cast Lancasters in the Russian Woolwich. Taking all these things into consideration, we ask, may we not find ourselves approaching the winter of 1855, and Sebastopol not yet taken. Meanwhile, all these preparations are going on, and before the season for operations commences, our unfortunate army will have been hung up to dry for six months in the north winds, like the souls tion of " Tartaru," we suppose, in or- of the departed in Virgil's descripder to extract from their bodies the foul miasma which those who yet survive have absorbed during their four months' residence in the valley of Devna, called by the Turks that of Death. God help our poor fellows! for we grieve to say that England, at least as represented by her press, seems inclined to sacrifice them, for the purpose of keeping in a place a most incompetent and mischievous set of men, simply because they are squeezable, and that every knot and faction of politicians in the land can coerce them into doing what-

ever these little knots and factions deem advisable for their own petty and individual interests. Enough for to-day. We conclude with recommending all whom our words may sary results of letting bygones," and reach, to reflect deeply upon the neces- " gones" plea they of will find amongst the " by- the coming year the honour of England, the alliance of France, and the existence of the Turkish empire.

For llie "Avis." While we fully concur with " H's" view of the subject treated on in the last number of the St. Croix Avis, as a vindication of rational and innocent amusements generally, we must differ from bim in so far as to the manner in which lie has directed his shaft ; being so obliquely aimed, it cannot effect much by way of suppressing the spirit of a flippant ranting meddler. Arrogance and pride in tlie general conduct of some persons are frequently the immediate productions of undue adulations bestowed upon tliern, which their peculiar position in the community renders difficult to detect ; every one's eyes being blinded by appearances, and much trouble not being taken to investigate more closely the true worth of such persons. No position, perhaps, offers a better opportunity to such selfesteemers to give vent to their hauteur and arrogancy than that of one fancying himself to be highly poised in the estimation of a community, as a popular preacher; for it is not unfrequently the case, that such men, regardless of every thing else, suppose that they can carry every thing before them by their tarmagant spirit and ranting eloquence. This, of course, the uninitiated will readily call zeal ; and the poor man himself buoyed in the idea that he is the great Champion of some approaching reformation, in consequence of large crowds attending upon his discourses, very few of whom are able to value them at thenreal price, often makes such encroachments on the boundaries of prudence

and discretion, as at last to evince, even to the most ignorant minds, bis presumption and self-esteem. Such is the light in which we are tempted to view the teacher-preacher, who, it lie bad exercised one grain of common sense in the selection of his last discourse, would never have directed his shaft at a private party, whose moral and religious eharacteras connected with the private entertainment given on Saturday evening last we defy him to impeach. There was but one of the party to whom anything by way of reprimand could he directed, if we admit of any propriety in doing so, (and most certainly we do not) ; hut then we would question very strictly his authority to reprimand that one. To vociferate then in the manner that the teacher-preacher did on Sunday evening last from the pulpit, when lie intended to correct a supposed evil in the conduct of one individual, is a fair specimen to t lie community of the soundness of his judgement and the refinement of his manners. To the best of our knowledge our assailant was not a witness of the performance in question, and that he could, notwithstanding his absence, know all those persons who were performing, proves that his ears are not deaf to talebearing, the pernicious effects of which, we trust, arc not unknown to him. If men of sound judgment, pastors of the other denominations, did not find it their dnty to meddle with the private entertainment of a select party, conducted with all decorum and propriety, what

right had our Champion to interfere in a matter which did not concern him? ; Let him, however, understand that we are free to act, and that in the exercise of that judgment which we possess, we will never yield to such usurpation over our conscience ; and that he can never render the Word beneficial to any of his hearers when so misused as on Sunday evening last, under the plea of preaching the gospel. A T 1 a From the St. Lucia Palladium December 1 0. ANTIGUA. A considerable period must elapse ere the Industrial Exhibition, recently held in this City, will cease to be the topic of conversation. The acknowledged success which has attended the first earnest effort to give prominency to the island's industry þÿ success which was achieved amidst much discouragement, arising from general distrust of the practicability of the scheme þÿ will certainly fill the most interesting pages of the Island's history, should a tropical Gibbon or another Edwards arise to chronicle events occurring in this section of the globe. But the gratifying details will not, unfortunately, go down to posterity, unaccompanied by others of an unpleasant character. The Press, in its fearless integrity, and regard for truthful narration, while disseminating far and wide the triumph of the projectors of the undertaking over all the obstacles which they had to encounter, has not attempted to conceal the fact, that by the Personage, in rank most exalted in the land, such discountenance has been evinced, as, if not counteracted by other and still more powerful influences, might seriously affect future attempts to promote so worthy a cause. The aptitude of the multitude to imitate the actions, and adopt the sentiments of those above them in station, invests all exalted positions with an amount of responsibility which, unhappily, is too much disregarded hy the eleve in society here and elsewhere ; and it is in dread of this danger-

ous influence, that the strange proceeding of Mr. Mcintosh with reference to the Exhibition, has called forth so much deserved censure. But notwithstanding we, i.i common with our brethren of the local journals, have not shrunk from the duly devolving upon us of animadverting in fitting terms on the conduct of the Executive, the Press, satisfied that the bane and antidote being both before the people, little real harm could accrue, would not have further pursued the ungracious theme, and popular ferment might ere this have subsided, was it not that the þÿ subject is still pertinaciously agitated by the indiscreet zeal of a few adherents of flie Governor, the ill judged defence of whom has only had the effect of furt her increasing his unpopularity. Twice, we learn, have attempts been made by certain members of the Executive Committee, personal friends of Mr. Mcintosh, (gentlemen, who hy the way, if only on account of their would-be- supposed social influence with that eccentric character, were originally most deeply mortified) to get up an address to His Excellency, condemnatory of the Press for giving publicity to facts which cannot be refuted, and professing perfect contentedness with the explanation which, it is said, his Excellency has made with reference to the grotesque costume in which he appeared at the Exhibition. The address, fulsome in its adulation, and disingenous in its avowals, was we are glad to say, rejected by the committee. But the intemperate and ill advised

subsequent acts of the Governor himself, has inflamed still further popular ill feeling against him. His' Excellency, furious at the strictures elicited from all quarters, and feeling himself impotent to curtail the independence and liberty of the Press, has stooped to the littleness of seeking to avenge himself on individuals, who, happening to hold public offices, may be, to a certain extent, exposed to the effects of his displeasure. We have heard of his unjustifiably assailing one Gentleman, who happened to be a member of the Executive Committee, an assault which though confined to

words, was said to be of a most violent character; and we know of a letter addressed officially to Mr. William Thibou, in his capacity of Justice of the Peace, instituting inquisitorial enquiries into the nature of his connection with this Journal, the extent of his interest in it either as Proprietor or Censor, and, as plainly as official reserve would permit, indicating to the gentleman that his commission, held with becoming dignity, and universal approbation for a period of seventeen years, would not be long suffered to remain in his honourable keeping, could it be only established, that he was guilty of the high crime of exercising his private judgment in approval of the views expressed by the Editor, or even could such negative treason be brought homo to him, as that of withholding the restraining authority he is strangely supposed to possess, over the free and honest expression of sentiments, when such sentiments happened to he d stasteful to the illustrious individual, who, for the punishment doubtless of the past sins of this community, holds dominion here. The correspondence which, it is said, took place between His Excellency and Mr. Thibou is not before the public, we are unable therefore to deal with it as we might otherwise have done, nor do we learn that his Excellency has yet further outraged public decency þÿ threat in effect; sufficient however has by carrying his imlied been attempted to prove that it is fortunate for this community that the power

of Governor Mcintosh must on this occasion be limited to a little harmless vapouring which, in being emitted, can only disagreeably affect him, from whom it proceeds. For this Journal we may say, that if by the fearless enunciation of opinions, held in common with all hut some half dozen officials, or as many sycophantic aspirants for social distinctions, we have chanced to cause Folly in high places to blush, and Absurdity to be ashamed, we will congratulate ourself on having, like the Venetian Moor, essentially ."done the state some service." þÿ Observer.

The following cure for the gout is taken from an old work : " First the person must pick a handkerchief frtun the pocket of a maid of fifty years, who has never had a wish to change her condition. Second, he must wash it in an honest miller's pond. Third, he must dry it on a parson's hedge who was never covetous. Fourth, lie must send it to a doctor's shop who never killed a patient. Fifth, he must mark it with a lawyer's ink who never cheated a client. Sixth, apply it to the part affected, and a cure will speedily follow."

GIVP THE SOLDIER A CHANCE. That in the þÿcaptain s but a choleric word Which in the soldier is rank þÿblasphemy. An additional step has been taken in the right direction as regards the soldier, mid on a principle entirely conformable with justice, and likely to produce very serviceable results. Last þÿTuesday Ga- s zette, tiller recording many well-earned promotions in the higher ranks of the army, contained a þÿ memorandum, to the eflect that one sergeant of every regiment of horse or foot serving in the | Crimea should receive a commission, to be (lilted from the battle of Inkerman, and this was followed by a warrant, extending considerably the provisions already existing for granting annuities and gratuities. One sergeant in every regiment is to be selected for an annuity of £20, and one sergeant, two corporals, and four privates in every regiment of cavalry, with one sergeant, four corporals, and ten privates in every regiment of infantry, are to be recommended for medals, and for gratuities, according to their respective ranks, of £15, þÿ ¬10, and t'5. These immediate and personal rewards for distinguished service are extremely desirable, for it cannot be altogether sufficient to tell a soldier that he shall be clothed when he is well, and tended when he is sick, or that his representatives will meet with benevolent consideration in case of his death. Such conduct as our troops have displayed deserves some honourable recognition which may be felt by the men them-

selves ; and there could obviously be none more consistent with military feeling than that which is conveyed by declarations and promotions. It is not, however, to be denied that the constitution of our army, in which officers and men are systematically taken from very different classes of society, may render considerable judgment necessary in carrying these laudable intentions into effect. A sergeant promoted for his good conduct would probably be some thirty years of age, and it may be presumed, with no means beyond his pay. Ilis step would place him on a level with a young gentleman of 18 or I!), possessing usually a certain amount of private income, and living accordingly. In short, whereas the steps from private to corporal, and corporal to sergeant, imply so many clear successive gains, that from sergeant to ensign or cornet may possibly involve a practical loss. So strongly has this been felt at different times that the question has been treated as one of considerable doubt, and Lord (Lev suggested, as tin improvement on the system now in use, that non-commissioned officers, when promoted for good

« ut tJ'I'JL A T a 3. conduct, should, instead of being made ensigns, receive the rank of captain tit once. The principle and motive of this suggestion we entirely appreciate; but would it not lie rather strange if when tin ensign and a sergeant were to be rewarded, tis might often happen, for gallantry in the same action, the ensign were to be made only a lieutenant and the sergeant a captain ? The solution of the difficulty may lie found in a variety of conditions resulting from the events of war. The improvement in the condition of the private soldier would in itself be a great aid in the matter, and it is reasonable to presume that the exigencies of active service would have material influence in destroying the coxcombry and extravagance incidental to military idleness. The distance between the sergeant and the ensign might lie insensibly lessened by the common perils and hardships of the field, and it, as is not improbable, the proposed promotions should take place in any considerable numbers, a class of officers would be formed able to hold its own with more effect than two or three isolated individuals. Beyond doubt, the courage and conduct of our officers has redounded to their infinite credit, and rendered it hard to impeach in any respect whatever the system of the British army; but nobody can believe that the admission to their ranks of such men as have recently been fighting by their side can lie otherwise than beneficial to the country, and honourable to the profes-

sion of arms. An Odessa correspondent ( Freuu/en Watt) writes that a train of several hundre Is ol waggons, laden with provisions and munitions for the Russian troops at Bakshiserai, was þÿ surprised by the frightful snowstorms in the steppes south of Perekop, and þÿannihilated. Sebastopol is provisioned for not more than fourteen or sixteen weeks, and the Russian relieving army altogether depends for its support upon the supplies sent from Southern Russia. These are conveyed in all descriptions of vehicles, principally drawn by oxen, which are as much exposed to destruction in the Taurian steppes as the ships of the allies in the Black Sea.

WHAT IS PASSING IN ST. PETERSBURG. The following private letter, dated the 8th inst., has been received from St. Petersburg : þÿ þÿ In consequence of the receipt of the affair of the 5th of November the Empress has had a serious and even alarming relapse. The courier found the Emperor in the apartment of the Empress, awaiting the news with feverish impatience; and when the truth was declared to him, he could not restrain his feelings, but broke out in the strongest expression of dissatisfaction and anger against his generals and his army. One exclamation which escaped him respecting his sons greatly alarmed the Empress, who was aware that they were with the army at Sebastopol ; she feared that some terrible calamity had befallen them seeing the agitation of her husband, and she fainted away. She remained for some time insensible ; and it was with much difficulty that the Emperor and the attendants succeeded in restoring her to animation. She became more calm when informed that nothing had occurred to her sons; but her health has seriously suffered from the check caused by the defeat of the army at Inkerman, and she has now to struggle against an increase of debility and low fever. The

greatest alarm is felt for her, and her deed. The solemnities very recovery is considered of the anniver- doubtful insary of the accession to the crown was very limited this year ; they were confined to a mere religious service in the churches. Amid the fears which the presence of the allied fleets has occasioned us, and the danger they yet menace, you can scarcely have an idea of the desperate efforts making here to complete the armaments of every kind for next spring. The Grand Duke Constantine takes no repose. He is at one moment in the arsenals of St. Petersburg, again at Sweaborg, and then at Cronstadt ; inspectingeverywhere, fleets, arsenals, foundries, and all the troops connected with those departments. The Emperor is often obliged to moderate this excessive ardour, in order to avoid alarming the population. We have several ships of flic line in the Admiralty docks, the screws for which are already advanced in execution. Of the guard þÿ(d elite) we have here at this moment only the regiment of Preobrnshenski, with its reserve battalions. Of the rest, two divisions are on the march for Poland, and the third is partitioned in the Baltic provinces. The letters we receive from the Crimea relative to the disasters caused by the hurricane of the l ltli, stale that the corps of Mannenberg, a part of which was en route for Bakshiserai, has suffered particularly. Their condition is of (fie most frightful kind from want of provisions as well as from the tempest. Many chiefs of divisions
who had been wounded in the affair of the 5th have died of their hurts.

A þÿDUTCHMAN S WILL. One of the most opulent of the Amone Mynheer Van der sterdam capitalists died a few days ago, B þÿ . Like many of his class, he was during his lifetime very careful not to disclose to any the amount of his possessions. On this point he even would not confide in his notary. Thus, when þÿ this worthy Dutchman a Roman Catho- a few years ago lic þÿ made his will, he resolved not to permit even his professional adviser to iiave anything to do in its composition. In the privacy of his own cabinet he made such a division of his almost fabulous wealth as he deemed right. The document þÿ his last will and testament þÿ he then placed in an envelope, sealed it with his own signet, and transferred it to the archives of his notary, by whom (and four witnesses, as the law requires) it was signed, registered, and duly legalised as the will of the individual whose signature it bore. On his death bed he communicated to certain of his friends the fact that one of the items in his will was 250 florins as a legacy for every Roman Catholic priest residing in Amsterdam. This was no great tax upon the good þÿman heirs, s and Mother Church required some proof of affection from her dying son. He died shortly after, and the will was opened. But the shrewdness even of a Dutch capitalist had been deceived. The Roman Catholic þÿ priests were not mentioned in the document þÿ that word had by some accident escaped the þÿwriter spen þÿ þÿ 1 give and bequeath to every Roman and

Catliolic (priests, of course, included,) residing in Amsterdam at the time of my decease, the sum of 250 þÿflorins, or words to that effect, trilled on the astonished ears of the late þÿcapitalist s children, as the notary read to them their þÿfather will. s Legal proceedings have been instituted by the family to obtain a rule against the enforcement of the will, but, as the error cannot be proved, the writer of it was never afflicted with an þÿhour insanity, s and his property will far more than meet all the claims resulting from this singular accident, it is not probable the plaintiffs will obtain a verdict. Several claims have already been made, and it will require about twelve millions of florins to carry out the literal conditions of the will. However, forty or fifty millions, it is said, will still be left as a consolation for this injured family.

SUFFERINGS OF THE TROOPS. from an infantry officer. J Camp above Sebastopol, Nov. 28. We landed from the Queen of the South last Tuesday, and were first ordered to encamp near Balaklava, but I had no sooner marched up to the ground indicated, about a mile from the bay, and got all ready for the tents, than an orderly came up with orders that we were to march up to the front that night. We, accordingly, got our packs on again, unpiled arms, and marched back to the beach, where I found the rest of the detachments all going up to the ground we had just left, and where they passed the night. We got our ammunition served out to us, loaded our pistols, and began the weary march at about twelve þÿo clock. Balaklava was, I dare say, before the demon of war entered it, a very pretty little town. Even now its situation is beautiful ; the harbour very small, but completely landlocked, with high mountains on each side, those on the right, looking up the country, occupied by the Highlanders and marines, facing the Russians. Their outposts are not a mile from each other. We marched up the road through the valley where the cavalry action took

3 tr US A T U 3 | dreadful, place on the 25th ; the road was most up to the knees in mud, and encumbered with dead bodies of mules, bullocks, and horses. What a sight this place would be for some enthusiastic member of the Humane Society ! French and Turkish troops were marching in every direction ; arabas, laden with provisions, to supply the wants of the immense army surrounding the place. Well, we proceeded on as best we could through the mud, till dark, and to every inquiry þÿ was. Five þÿmiles was the invariable as to how far the Third Division answer. As it became perfectly dark we began to suspect that our guide, an orderly of the I3th Dragoons, did not know much about the country. At last we reached a French camp, and asked them where the English were. They guided us to a camp, and, to our great dismay, we found we were among the Light Division, on the extreme right of the whole position, about tour miles beyond our eamp.

We copy from the St. Thomas Times, the following correspondence, relative to the unpleasant affair of the þÿ lienjamin Franklin Our readers will be able to judge of the affair. It must, however, be recollected that the Steamer left the harbor of St. Thomas after Sun-set without a night pass; consequently at variance with the harbor-regulations. She was only chartered to convey the Mails, and could not be considered one of the regular Mail Steamers; therefore, the captain or consignee should not have neglected to conform to the regulations.

From the New York Tribune, January !. Major Helm to (lor. Berg. Commercial Agency of the U. S. of A., ) At the Island of St. Thomas, Dec. 23, 1854. $ Sir : I have the honor to inform you that J. N Olcott, Esq., has jnst placed me in possession of the facts relative to the late outrage perpetrated by one of your subordinates on the American steamer Benjam m Franklin , her crew and passengers, which it becomes my duty to communicate to you officially. The Royal Mail Steam Packet Parana, from Southampton, with the West India Mails, and some 200 passengers, was delayed some days on her passage out, and the Agent of that Company, Mr. Cameron, dispatched the windward and leeward steamers a few hours before her arrival. In the absence of a steamer of the Company, Mr. Cameron chartered the American steamer Benjamin Franklin to take the mails and passengers to Barbados, and other windward islands. The Benjamin Franklin was properly cleared at the Custom House and port ns an American steamer, chartered by the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, and during the afternoon of the 21st inst., had the American flag and signal of the It. M. S. I Company flying. The Collector of Customs and Postmaster of this Island is the same person At about 3 o'clock the clearance was granted,

dL and after sunset the same person who granted the 1 clearance, or one of his subordinates, placed on board the mails. The vessel was detained until about 8 þÿo clock P. M., in taking on passengers and baggage. When she got under way, in passing the western fort, a blank cartridge was fired at her, when she immediately stopped her engines, and, as soon as practicable, backed in to ascertain the cause of the shot being fired ; and, while in the act of returning, three balls were fired at her in quick þÿsuccession there being only a few seconds between each. The first missed ; the second struck and damaged the vessel, shattering several plank, and breaking and injuring everything in a stateroom on the starboard quarter, in which were a lady and child, who miraculously' escaped uninjured ; the third shot passed immediately over the vessel, and within a foot of the heads of two of the officers. The vessel came into the harbor and anchored until about 2 þÿo clock on yesterday, to repair temporarily the damage, when she again set sail with mails and passengers. Immediately after the shots were fired, Mr. Cameron addressed a note to your subordinate, Major Castonier, in command of the Forts, to inquire the cause of this unexpected and extraordinary proceeding, and the next morning received in reply, a note in keeping with the outrage itself, which is in the following words : þÿ Fort Christian, Friday, Dec. 22, 1854. þÿ Sir : I had not received the report from the Battery when I last evening got your note. 1 am

now able to inform you that it was the steamer Benjamin Franklin that was stopped by the western battery for leaving the harbor after dark without special permission. þÿ Had the Fort been informed that this suspected and here long-detained vessel had been employed to carry the mails, she would have been treated like one of the R. M. S. þÿCompany ves- s sels, and no mistake could have occurred. However, she was not detained long. I remain, Sir, Your most obedient servant, FK CASTONIER

To Cameron, þÿEsq. The American steamer Benjamin Franklin was attempted to be detained at New York by the Venezuelan Consul, and the Fnitcd States Court, at his instance, sent a Commission on board, who, after an examination, made their report to the Court, when the vessel was permitted to clear regularly for the þÿI ort of St. Thomas, carrying with her an American Register and Flag, evidence to this Government as well as to myselt of her nationality. That she has been detained here as a suspected vessel is not true, as Your Excellency well knows. The remark, that þÿ had the Fort been informed þÿ that she was employed to carry the mails, she þÿ would have been treated as one of the R. M. þÿ 8. þÿCompany svessels, and no mistake could þÿ have þÿoccurred is a prevarication , and an attempt to add insult to outrage. Your subordinate, Major Castonier, either did know, or was it his duty to have known, that this vessel had been employed earry to the mails, and hence, under your regulations, required no þÿ night signatures as to its correctness, I would, þÿpass. 1 am fortified in the belief that Major Castonier did know the fact, from the statements of Mr. Cameron and the Harbor Master, herewith enclosed, which, in terms, contradict the implied statement of Major Castonier, that the fort had not been notified. The vessel was cleared at the Custom House for the purpose of carrying the mails, and the Custom House Officer, who is also Postmaster, placed them on board. The vessel, from about 3 þÿo clock , had signal the of the
Mail Company flying almost under the nose of Major Castonier, and placards were posted up the Custom House and Post Office, stating that the mails would be dispatched on this vessel.

But, Sir, had this vessel attempted to leave the harbor without being cleared at all, the outrage would have been equally great ; for you have already received, through the British Consul, the statement of the officers of the vessel and thirty four passengers, among whom are the Governor of St. Vincent, and the Lord Bishop of British Guiana, who state that instantly upon firing the first shot the vessel stopped ; what more could she do than obey the summons ? Nothing Ibid she been an enemy at war, instead of a peaceable mail-boat, it would have been an outrage, condemned by all civilized nations, to have fired into her after she had obeyed the summons ; yet, Sir, three balls were fired at and into this vessel, after she had stopped, endangering the lives of the crow and passengers, and Major Castonier replies, However, she. was not detained þÿlong. þÿ 1 must, therefore, request that Mr. Olcott, the owner of the American steamer, be reimbursed for his expenditures and other damage incurred by reason of this illegal and extraordinary act of your subordinate. 1 also deem it a duty to say to your Excellency, who has universally exhibited a friendly feeling not only to myself personally, but to my Government, and a justice and impartiality which command my highest respect as well as friendship, that, under the circumstances, 1 am impelled by a sense of duty to forward all the facts to the Government of the U. States, with a request that a demand be made upon the Danish Government

for the dismissal of your subordinate officer, who, with a recklessness unparalleled, and without the shadow of cause, exposed the lives of thirty American seamen, and some sixty passengers, together with a valuable American steamer to imminent peril. 1 am, Sir, Very respectfully, Your þÿob þÿserv t. t., CH. Governor Jierg's reply to Major Helm. Government House, St. Thomas 23d Dec. 1854. Sir : I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your esteemed letter of this day, with inclosure, respecting the firing, from the Western Point battery, upon the American steamer Benjamin Franklin, hired by the R. M. S P. Co. I do most sincerely regret this very disagreable occurrence, which the reports of the fort and battery state to be owing to the ship leaving after dark, without requisite special permission, and not ascribable to any fault on their side. I have, however, already ordered the matter to be investigated by a Military Court of Inquiry, and beg to assure you that nothing shall be wanting on my part, to bring the matter to a just and satisfactory conclusion. I have the honor to be, Sir, very respectfully, your obedient servant, IT. II. BERG. To Cii. J. Helm, U. S Agent at St. Thomas.

FROM THE SEAT OF WAR. ST. PETERSBURG, Jan. 10. Great distress is experienced in this city, and much dissatisfaction prevails at the hardships imposed by tlie war. In all the churches prayers are now offered for peace. As religious services in Russia are subject to the direct control of the Government, this fact is significant. The Journal tie St. Petersburg of the 3d, gives one-fourth of its news columns to the report of Mr. þÿBright spro-Russian speech, delivered on the22d ult., in the House of Commons. ODESSA, Jan. 3. Some 360 men belonging to a regiment offoot, and several hundred Jewish carriers, perished in a snow-storm, on the 22d of December, at no great dis- | tance from this city. The cause of the misfortune was, that a sudden frost set | in after the þÿmen s clothes had got wet through. A thick rind or crust of ice having speedily formed on their clothing, the men huddled together in groups of 20 and 30, in order to keep each other warm, but when found they were all lifeless. The blockade of Odessa is a mere myth, but trade is completely stagnant. þÿ'i he transport of troops and munitions of war has become impossible, the roads being impassable. By the retrograde movement of the Turkish army the Russian troops in Bessarabia seem to have felt relief, for some strong detachments have been sent off in forced marches to the Crimea.
SPEECH OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS NAPOLEON. The Moniteur says: þÿ This day (Tuesday), at noon, the Emperor, attended by the Minister of War, and Generals Reg-

nault de St. Jean þÿd Angely, ltolin de Cotte, and Mellinet, reviewed, in the court of honour before the Tuileries, the detachments of the Imperial Guard, destined to join the army of the East in the Crimea, and whose departure will take place on the 10th or lltli of this month. These troops, under the command of General Ulrich, were composed of one company of Sappers of the Engineers, of detachments from the 1st and 2d Regiments of Grenadiers, of detachments from the 1st and 2d Regiments of Volti geurs, of a half battalion of the Foot Chasseurs, and two batteries of Horse Artillery. The infantry was arrayed in three lines, with the artillery behind it. Ilis Majesty, after passing down the front of the troops, stationed himself near the Clock Pavilion, where the battalions were formed in square. The Emperor advanced to the centre, and pronounced the following address m a firm and fervent tone of voice, amid repeated cries of þÿ Vive þÿl Empereur þÿ Soldiers, The French people in the þÿ sovereignty of their will have set up again many things deemed for ever dead, and now the empire is reconstituted, Intimate alliances exist with our former enemies. The Hag of France waves with honour on distant shores, which until now the bold flight of our eagles has never reached. The Imperial Guard, the heroic representative of military glory and honour, is here before me, surrounding the Emperor as of yore, wearing the same uniform, carrying the same flag, and, above all, cherishing in

its heart the same feelings of devotion to its country. Receive then these flags, which will lead you on to victory, as they led your fathers, as they have just led your comrades. Go and share what dangers yet remain to be surmounted, what glory to be gathered. Soon you will have received the noble baptism to which you aspire, and you will have helped to plant our eagles on the walls of þÿSebastopol. After this harangue, the Emperor alighted from his horse, and with his own hand gave the flags to the two colonels commanding the Grenadiers and the Voltigeurs. Her Majesty, the Empress, present in the balcony, then descended into the square and walked round it, leaning on the arm of the Emperor. Their Majesties stopped several times to speak to the soldiers. Seeing the emotion of the Empress, these warriors redoubled tlieii enthusiastic cries. 'Pile Emperor, aftci conducting the Empress hack, remounted Ins horse, and the ranks began to defile past him. A considerable crowd pressed against the iron railing of the Carrousel, and mingled their acclamations with those ol the soldiery. All the spectators admired the martial air and ardour of these fine troops. þÿ Ibid,

Marshal Vaillant, French Minister of War, has received the following report, dated Dec. 22, 1854, from General Canrobert : þÿ þÿ Monsieur le Marechal: The had weather has been prolonged until now, with rare and liriet intervals of improvement; nevertheless we continue as much as possible the work of inclosing the place with our trenches, and, although the rains make the movement of vehicles .difficult, the siege works are growing to completeness and consolidation. þÿ The two armies reciprocally assist each other. To the English army I am indebted for the conveyance, by water, of nearly all the cavalry at my disposal in the Crimea ; and on my part, 1 have placed at Lord þÿRaglan his horses for removing disposal s sick to Bala- sumpter klava, and teams for the conveyance of his supplies. These exchanges contribute to keep up excellent relations and perfect cordiality between the two armies. þÿ Hardly a night passes in which our advanced works are not attacked in a sortie of the enemy. These attempts generally cost the assailants dear. Yesterday, at two þÿo clock in the morning, the Russians, after making a sortie against the third parallel of the English, a who . vigorously repulsed them, made similar demonstration against the centre and left of our works. Received with a very lively and well-directed fire, they retired before our soldiers, who pursued them with the bayonet. The enemy left a great number of dead upon the field. þÿ In order to render the protection of the trenches more efficient, I have organ-

ised a corps of volunteers, whose peculiar duty it is to reconnoitre the approaches to our works during the night. This institution completes that of the sharpshooters (francs tireurs) organised at the commencement of the siege, and who do duty by day in our trenches themselves. They have already done a great deal of harm to the enemy. þÿ As l have already announced to you, our works now extend to the bottom of the Quarantine bay. The enemy shows that he is not inattentive to our progress on that side, and his guns hotly dispute the ground with us, where we are obliged, as we are nearly everywhere, to dig into the solid rock. But our progress is not the less real, and we remain in possession. þÿ I have already informed you that the enemy has withdrawn his left, and evacuated those points in the valley of Balaklava where we had previously seen him in large masses. The day before yesterday, wishing to ascertain the situation he had taken up in that direction, I sent out a force consisting of a cavalry brigade, under the command of General þÿd Allonville, to reconnotrie as far as the village of Tchourgouna. Behind the village of Kamara they fell in with a few hundred sharpshooters, whom they drove hack into the ravines. Some groups of cavalry, accompanied by their artillery, and a few battalions of infantry, appeared on the flanks of the party making the reconnoissance, but they did not attempt to offer any opposition to the operation of the latter, which was most successfully executed.

þÿ At the same time, 1,000 foot soldiers, Highlanders and Zouaves, left Balaklava to the right of our positions, and explored the of heights the valley Baidari. They only met a that extend towards post of Cossacks.

; a\ <e ® © a sc at s. þÿ In fine, I think that on the left bank of the Tchernaya the enemy has only a few soldiers posted to observe our positions at a distance. A movement has evidently been produced in the Russian army, the probable cause of which is the debarkation of the Turkish troops still going on at Eupatoria. I shall soon receive information on this head. þÿ Although the number of the sick has i slightly increased, in consequence of the constant dampness in which we live, the sanitary state of the army is satisfactory, and the moral spirit of the troops is perfect. þÿ Although the soldiers have been heavily inconvenienced by the rains, there has yet been no cold weather; the snow, which for a long time past has covered the tops of the mountains in the interior, has not appeared on the hillplain we occupy, and the thermometer has not once fallen below zero. These general conditions are improved by the care we take of our soldiers; and, thanks to the prudent foresight of the Emperor and his Government, the army enjoys a relative degree of comfort that makes it gaily support with a light heart its fatigues. þÿ The number of the sick in our military hospitals at Constantinople amounts to 3,794, of whom 1,387 are wounded. Out of this total, 260 are liussians. I have established a convalescent depot in the Crimea, near the Bay of Karateh. Here the men who leave the army ambulances, and who only require a little repose before they return to their duty, | will have their recovery promoted. This

measure will diminish our draughts to Constantinople. þÿ II. I. II. Prince Napoleon, still detained at Constantinople by the illness j authorized to import and sell that compelled him to leave the Crimea, wished to come and rejoin us. I was bound to oppose this return, which compromised the health of the þÿI rince. þÿ Accept &.C., (Signed) þÿ The General-in-Chief, þÿCanrobert.

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC AND UNITED STATES. The measure of annexing Santo Domingo does not find general approbation even in the United States, and perfect opposition at the place most interested in the question. With regard to the former assertion, I will only extract a short passage from the document which the members of Congress opposed to the Nebraska Bill issued as a manifesto to the people of the United States. It must he recollected that no less a personage than Mr. Solomon Foot, the member for Vermont, presided as chairman over the meeting, which was held at Washington, on the 2(Mhof June last, and the extract concerning Santo Domingo is worded as follows : þÿ Umuistakeable indications appear of a purpose to annex the eastern part of San Domingo, and to subjugate the whole island, restoring it to the dominion of slavery þÿ and this is to be followed up by an alliance with Brazil and the extension of slavery into the valley of the þÿAmazon. The presence of three French men-ofwar gives naturally great confidence to all foreigners residing here. It would no doubt have conduced to a feeling of I greater safety were there likewise one or two of her þÿMajesty ships s in front of the city of Santo Domingo. þÿ Ibid.
